A small decision head trained label-free can recover about 99% of a frozen language model's multiple-choice accuracy while using only two-thirds of its transformer layers. It learns the full model's answer probabilities with KL divergence, without correct-answer labels for training. One backbone pass reads the question and all options together; the head returns probabilities for every option. We call this model FunDM (Fun Decision Model). Using 24 of Qwen3-8B's 36 layers and skipping the LM head, its +1T variant reaches 75.0% mean accuracy over eight benchmarks, versus 75.7% for the full model. On MMLU-Pro, both heads achieve 1.56 to 1.57 times batched vLLM throughput with about one-third lower peak GPU allocator memory. Both heads score higher than released Contrastive Language Models (CLM), fine-tuned CLM, and CLM-shaped heads trained from scratch on the eight multiple-choice benchmarks and coding-agent selection. Separately trained agent heads learn judge probabilities without pass/fail labels and select passing runs for 74.4 to 74.6 of 100 held-out tasks on average, versus 74 for the full-model judge and 52.0 for a CLM-shaped action-trained head. Code is available at: https://github.com/Ujjawal-K-Panchal/FunDM
items.authors: Ujjawal K. Panchal

items.title: ModRes: A modification of the ResPlan dataset ready for floor plan analysis and graph machine learning
items.abstract: Floor plan datasets underpin computational analysis of building layouts, spatial connectivity and graph machine learning. However, publicly available datasets often require substantial preprocessing before they can be used reliably. We present ModRes, a cleaned and enriched version of the ResPlan dataset, containing 8,431 valid and unique residential floor plans. Invalid and duplicate floor plans are removed through a dedicated cleaning workflow, producing a ready-to-use dataset. For each floor plan, ModRes provides two-dimensional geometry, images, three-dimensional building representations and three complementary dual graphs in CSV and JSON formats with graph-, node- and edge-level features. Continuous and categorical graph attributes support machine learning workflows. We characterise the dataset using graph-based statistics and demonstrate its utility through a range of case studies. ModRes provides structured geometric, topological and semantic representations needed to automate spatial analysis and support machine learning-based workflows for building design and performance evaluation.
items.authors: Emma Shelley, Wassim Jabi, Thomas Woolley, Katerina Kaouri

items.title: CartoVec: General-Purpose Location Embeddings from Open Map Data
items.abstract: Geographic coordinates are common inputs in applied machine learning, but latitude and longitude describe position rather than the surrounding environment. Image-grounded location encoders learn this context from satellite or ground-level imagery; structured open map data offers another source of supervision whose utility for continuous coordinate encoders remains less explored. We introduce CartoVec, a coordinate encoder trained to predict Overture-derived land cover, land use, transportation, place and connectivity targets at multiple spatial scales, without image inputs or downstream-task labels. We evaluate frozen embeddings on Census outcomes, Airbnb prices and Philadelphia crime in the US Northeast using spatial block cross-validation. CartoVec has the highest mean performance on most Census outcomes and the highest average across the full suite, with several comparisons close across folds. The findings support open map data as a practical source of reusable location representations with a coordinate-to-vector interface that requires no map lookup at inference. The open-weight model is available at https://huggingface.co/gursoyfurkan/CartoVec.
items.authors: Furkan Gursoy

items.title: MLAfication: Efficiently Enabling High-Fidelity MLA for Modern LLMs
items.abstract: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) compresses the KV cache into a latent representation, reducing inference memory and bandwidth. Existing MHA2MLA/TransMLA methods do not support QKNorm and require costly recovery on modern LLMs, especially MoE. We present MLAfication, a QKNorm-compatible, parameter-efficient extension of MHA2MLA. It combines calibrated KNorm, parameter-efficient distillation, contribution-aware Partial-RoPE, and activation-aware joint KV initialization. Across MHA and GQA models, including QKNorm- and MoE-equipped variants, MLAfication preserves performance under substantial KV-cache compression, surpasses the current SOTA on commonsense and long-context benchmarks, and extends MLA conversion to modern architectures. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, MLAfication delivers up to $5.35\times$ the serving throughput of BF16 GQA and, combined with 4-bit KV quantization, reduces the KV-cache footprint by $94.73\%$. Our code is available at https://github.com/JT-Ushio/MLAfication.
items.authors: Zile Wang, Zhide Xie, Tao Ji

items.title: Online LLM Personalization from Pairwise Preferences Across Users
items.abstract: Large language models can answer the same question in different styles, but users' preferred styles are hidden and vary across users and questions. We study inference-time personalization through online selection from a fixed set of prompts, each representing a persona. Users arrive sequentially, each asks a short sequence of questions, and the system displays two responses per question and observes one pairwise choice. We formulate this interaction as a variant of the contextual dueling bandit problem in which the learner starts without preference data, adapts within each session, and exploits information shared across users. The objective is to minimize cumulative strong regret, summing the utility gaps of both displayed responses relative to the user's best response among the available options. We make two contributions. First, we introduce the problem and release a reproducible preference benchmark and dataset built around a tutoring case study, containing educational questions, LLM-generated answers in six teaching styles, and pairwise judgments from LLM-simulated students with hidden preference profiles. We fit Bradley-Terry models to these judgments to obtain reference utilities for regret evaluation. Second, we propose a baseline that learns a mixture prior over users from completed sessions and adapts to each new user within the session. On students and topics never used in development, it removes 44-48% of random pairs' excess regret and achieves over half the performance of a per-user linear oracle fitted in hindsight. We release code, prompts, and the benchmark.
items.authors: Romain Puech, Georgy Salakhutdinov, Dimitris Bertsimas

items.title: Density-Matrix Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: What information does a reinforcement learning policy omit? At each state, a standard policy stores one probability per action. It has no place to record how actions relate to each other, such as which pairs go together and which conflict. We ask when this missing structure matters, and we give exact answers. We store the policy at each state as a density matrix, a positive semidefinite, unit-trace matrix borrowed from quantum information theory. We use it here as a purely classical data structure, computed on ordinary classical hardware. The diagonal holds the usual action probabilities. The off-diagonal entries, called coherences, are new parameters. This gives density-matrix reinforcement learning (DMRL). Coherences change outcomes in two settings. First, suppose a policy is regularized toward a coherent reference policy using matrix relative entropy. The optimum then has coherences that no diagonal reference policy produces, and its action probabilities can depend on the reference policy's coherences. This is relevant to fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) with a Kullback--Leibler penalty. Second, suppose the agent chooses a unit-vector action and the reward is a quadratic function of that vector. This could arise when an LLM judge scores a weighted consolidation of reasoning paths, or when coupled robotic sensors each respond to a mix of actions. Then some coherent policies earn strictly more expected reward than every classical policy with the same action probabilities, and we give the margin in closed form. In a two-action example, both policies assign probability $0.5$ to each action, yet the classical one earns expected reward $0$ while the coherent one earns $1$, the maximum. Outside these two settings, DMRL matches or transfers the classical results. This is a theory paper. All results are proved, and we report no empirical evaluation.
items.authors: Chiuman Ho

items.title: CodeLift: Your Test Suite Is Secretly a Dense SWE Curriculum
items.abstract: The pass-all-test binary reward has become a standard recipe for training software engineering agents, but its sparsity eliminates difference of partially correct patches. The test pass-rate is a natural alternative. However, we find that it is not a reliable indicator of patch quality. A functionality being tested can be covered by either one challenging test or one hundred trivial tests, where the majority might be already satisfied pass-to-pass tests. We introduce CodeLift, a reinforcement learning method that dynamically calibrates pass-rate rewards, turning the test suite into an adaptive curriculum. At each iteration, CodeLift groups tests that kill the same patches and patches that pass the same tests, then gives more weight to test groups that fewer patch groups pass. This reduces the impact of majority simple tests and focuses more on what is still challenging. Within each rollout, CodeLift applies the same scoring rule to repository snapshots, assigning credit to useful actions even when later ones introduce regressions. Experiments on SWE benchmarks show that CodeLift consistently improves pass@1/2/4/8 over binary and pass-rate baselines. Analyses show that CodeLift provides dense, stable learning signals and unlocks the inherent curriculum in the test suite.
items.authors: Junjielong Xu, Huachao Zhu, Alyssa Wu, Zhichao Hu, Pinjia He

items.title: MIRRA: Fast, High-Fidelity Molecular Generation with Chemistry-Informed Discrete Flow Matching
items.abstract: Fast, high-fidelity molecular generation requires accurate chemical choices and efficient sampling. Chemical building blocks reduce graph size, but make each node a choice among tens of thousands of related identities. We introduce MIRRA (Molecular Identity Representation, Refresh and Assembly), a discrete flow-matching generator that learns from chemical knowledge and evaluates identity probabilities only when needed, while keeping every identity in its vocabulary available. Chemical features share information across related blocks, and learned identity corrections distinguish them in molecular context. By deciding which positions will refresh before computing their probabilities, the sampler avoids unused predictions while preserving each sampling transition. Against the strongest baselines in each task, MIRRA reduces chemical and graph distribution errors on ZINC250k by 29-31% and 53-60%, respectively, with generation up to 8.6 times faster. Property targeting yields an estimated 7.8-20.8 times more distinct novel hits per second. On a held-out polymer test set, MIRRA achieves 100% periodic validity with known chain topology, versus 57.0% for a polymer variational autoencoder. These results demonstrate fast, high-fidelity generation with the full chemical vocabulary available throughout sampling.
items.authors: Ge Sun, Juan J. de Pablo

items.title: LLM-to-Flow Distillation: Teaching Natural Language Goals to Scientific Generators
items.abstract: Generative discovery in science requires coupling high-level scientific reasoning with the ability to generate samples respecting the structure of a design space. Yet these capabilities remain largely separated: foundation LLMs encode broad chemical and biological knowledge, while domain-specific flow- and diffusion-based generators capture the priors needed to produce valid sequences and geometries. We study how to align such scientific generators to high-level natural-language discovery goals without requiring an explicit proxy reward, which is often unavailable or poorly captured by learned predictors in experimental sciences. We introduce LLM-to-Flow Distillation (LFD), where a frozen LLM acts as an adaptive teacher for a domain-specific generator. Given a goal such as 'generate peptides with promising anticancer activity', the teacher constructs a curriculum of intermediate sub-goals aware of the flow's current capabilities, and progressively directs them toward the original discovery goal. At each round, the LLM judges sampled candidates under the current objective. These judgments induce preferences that are iteratively distilled into the generator through DPO. This procedure provides dense learning signals even when the initial model places negligible probability on designs satisfying the final goal, enabling adaptation toward poorly covered, out-of-distribution regions. Experiments on therapeutic peptides and small-molecule structure design demonstrate that LFD enables a new form of generative control: aligning arbitrary domain-specific scientific generators to scientific discovery tasks expressed via high-level natural-language goals.
items.authors: Riccardo De Santi, Federico Di Gennaro, Angelo Gnazzo, Sophia Tang, Pranam Chatterjee, Fanny Yang, \.Ismail \.Ilkan Ceylan, Michael M. Bronstein, Andreas Krause

items.title: Protocol Choices Matter More Than the Aggregation Algorithm: Federated Learning for In-Hospital Mortality Prediction in Care-Unit and Multi-Hospital Federations
items.abstract: Federated learning allows hospitals to train a shared mortality model without pooling their records, but published comparisons of aggregation strategies rarely control the evaluation protocol. This study compared seven strategies (FedAvg, FedProx, SCAFFOLD, FedAdagrad, FedAdam, FedYogi and FedCluster) on two federations built with one pipeline: 12 care units of a hospital in MIMIC-IV and 49 hospitals in eICU-CRD. Each strategy was tuned and selected on validation data by the same rule, and every comparison was repeated across 10 seeds with Friedman and Holm-corrected tests. SCAFFOLD ranked first in both federations (AUC-ROC 0.886 and 0.819) and in 17 of 18 variants, but its margin over the runner-up never exceeded 0.008, and a control sharing its local optimizer attributed most of its margin over FedAvg to drift correction. On the multi-hospital federation, federated training matched centralized training. In the care-unit federation, three protocol choices changed discrimination by more than the choice of strategy did: discharge-coded predictors (+0.038 in AUC-ROC), client-level SMOTE (up to -0.074), and evaluating the last instead of the best validation round (up to -0.084). Platt scaling on validation data repaired the risks distorted by imbalance corrections without loss of discrimination. Studies should therefore fix the protocol before ranking algorithms.
items.authors: Rodrigo Tertulino, Ricardo Almeida, La\'ercio Alencar

items.title: The Surprising Expressivity of a Single Neuron with Autoregressive Chain-of-Thought
items.abstract: The success of autoregressive language models trained with Chain-of-Thought~(CoT) supervision raises a fundamental question: How simple can a next-token predictor be while still enabling the efficient simulation of general computation through its autoregressively generated CoT? Surprisingly, we show that a single neuron suffices. For a broad family of activations, including threshold and ReLU, a single autoregressive neuron can simulate any feedforward circuit with the same activation. Specifically, a size-$s$ circuit on $n$ inputs can be simulated by a neuron of dimension $O(ns+s^2)$ using $O(s^2)$ generation steps, with both bounds independent of circuit depth and tight under natural assumptions. For threshold activations, this improves upon the simulation of Joshi et al. (COLT 2025), whose bounds scale exponentially with circuit depth. Consequently, autoregressive threshold neurons can simulate polynomial-time Turing machines, while remaining efficiently learnable from CoT supervision. Our main expressivity result relies on a novel connection to Sidon sets from additive combinatorics. As an experimental illustration, we efficiently train a single autoregressive ReLU neuron to mimic a neural network teacher with nontrivial test accuracy on CIFAR-10.
items.authors: Roey Magen, Nirmit Joshi, Gal Vardi

items.title: Which Geometry on Which Layer? Measured Sign-Spectral Assignment in Mixed-Optimizer Training
items.abstract: Modern neural-network training uses mixed recipes, assigning AdamW-like or sign-based updates to embedding and output layers and spectral updates to hidden matrices. These assignments are usually fixed by layer type, without a clear criterion for selecting the appropriate geometry. We turn sign-versus-spectral assignment into a measurable, layerwise decision problem. For ideal memoryless steps, we derive a finite-batch ratio of conservative descent-lemma lower bounds for spectral and sign updates. Its closed form separates signal efficiency from a geometry-dependent global curvature factor. In the positive-signal regime, the same smoothness assumption gives two-sided bounds that determine which step has the larger conditional expected decrease when the ratio crosses explicit noise-dependent thresholds. We then derive a local directional quadratic score from gradient alignments and Hessian-vector products and use it in Generalized-Scion (G-Scion) to control layerwise routing. In a controlled input-rank experiment, including directional curvature matches the measured same-iterate ordering in all seven aggregate settings, whereas the curvature-free proxy selects the opposite geometry. On 31M GPT-2, the output score routes the output layer from spectral warmup to sign, and G-Scion improves validation loss over fixed Scion in memoryless and matched-momentum comparisons. ViT-B/16 results further show that a spectral edge assignment can outperform fixed Scion outside language modelling. These results suggest that optimizer geometry need not be hard-coded by layer type and are a first step toward understanding how it should be assigned.
items.authors: Hiroki Naganuma, Laura Gomezjurado, Mahdi Ghaznavi, Ganesh Talluri, Atsushi Nitanda, Seng Pei Liew, Ryuichiro Hataya, Ioannis Mitliagkas

items.title: A Geometrical Approach to Constructing Neural Networks for Perfect Training-set Classification
items.abstract: This paper proposes a method for constructing a neural network that achieves perfect classification of all samples in a given training set, without taking regularization into account. The network is constructed on-demand, with its layer sizes and neuron parameters determined through a geometrical analysis of the input data, in which separating hyperplanes are created and mapped to neurons with step activation functions. The proposed architecture consists of two hidden layers with distinct roles: inter-class separation and transformation of the data into a linearly separable representation. Inter-class separation requires every bi-chromatic pair of samples belonging to different classes to be separated by at least one hyperplane. We show that when this separation is achieved through a hierarchical partitioning of the data, the leaf nodes of the oblique decision tree, obtained as a byproduct, directly define the neurons of the linear separability layer, whose size is only one neuron greater than that of the inter-class separation layer. Experiments on the MNIST dataset demonstrate that the proposed method achieves perfect training-set classification, and compact models. The direct correspondence between the decision tree and network neurons enhances interpretability and explainability, while the construction procedure offers opportunities for parallel implementation and improved scalability.
items.authors: Akos Hajnal

items.title: Near-Optimal Regret Bounds for Monotone Stochastic Optimization under Semi-Bandit Feedback
items.abstract: Stochastic optimization models sequential decision-making under uncertainty, typically assuming known input distributions. When these distributions are unknown, \citet{agarwal2026semibandit} give an online-to-offline reduction for monotone stochastic optimization under semi-bandit feedback, where only probed variables are observed. Its expected regret relative to the offline guarantee is $\widetilde O(n\sqrt T)$, where $n$ is the number of variables and $T$ the horizon. For optimal stopping and Pandora's box, \citet{liu2025improved} achieve $\widetilde O(\sqrt{nT})$ using problem-specific algorithms. \emph{Can a general online-to-offline reduction achieve this improved rate?} We give such a reduction for strongly monotone stochastic optimization, answering the corresponding open question. Strong monotonicity is defined relative to the chosen offline algorithm. Our oracle-efficient reduction achieves $\widetilde O(\sqrt{nT})$ expected regret while preserving approximation guarantees for oracles satisfying the same condition. It combines Bernstein-type optimistic distribution estimates with a Hellinger stability bound for adaptive policy transcripts, aggregating squared marginal errors weighted by the executed policy's probing probabilities. The rate is optimal up to logarithmic factors for $T\ge n$, even under full feedback. Under monotonicity and uniformly bounded coordinate-wise variation, the same algorithm achieves $\widetilde O(n^{3/4}\sqrt T)$ expected approximation regret, improving the previous linear dependence on $n$. The exponent $3/4$ is sharp for its ordinary regret over instances and exact oracle choices. Our framework applies to prophet inequality, Pandora's box, best-of-$K$ selection, stochastic knapsack, stochastic orienteering, and stochastic submodular maximization.
items.authors: Tao Hu, Rohan Ghuge

items.title: COMPASS: Membership Inference Attack Against Vision Large Language Models via Adaptive Noise Calibration
items.abstract: Vision large language models (VLLMs) are deployed in privacy-sensitive domains, raising training-data exposure concerns. Existing gray-box membership inference attacks (MIAs) commonly rely on entropy statistics or generated descriptions, requiring costly generation with limited membership separation. Perturbation-based methods instead measure response changes but focus on large perturbations, leaving VLLM membership behavior under smaller perturbations poorly understood. We systematically characterize VLLM membership behavior under controlled Gaussian perturbations across noise levels at fine resolution. We find that optimal perturbation magnitude and membership-signal direction vary across model-dataset pairs. In many settings, a previously unstudied low-noise regime yields stronger separation than large perturbations, with members exhibiting lower divergence than non-members, reversing the conventional score direction. Other settings retain the conventional direction, demonstrating that neither a fixed perturbation magnitude nor a predetermined score orientation is universally reliable. We propose COMPASS, an adaptive gray-box MIA that calibrates both the perturbation magnitude and membership-score direction using a loosely distribution-matched, known non-member reference set. We instantiate COMPASS using Renyi-normalized KL divergence and Renyi divergence, with max-k aggregation over the most informative image-logit positions. Across LLaVA v1.5-7B, MiniGPT-4, and HuluMed-32B, spanning pretraining, instruction-tuning, and medical-image datasets, COMPASS outperforms baselines. On general-domain data, COMPASS achieves AUCs up to 0.88. On the distribution-matched medical evaluation, it reaches 0.64 AUC, while the strongest baseline remains at chance level. These results establish full-range adaptive perturbation analysis as an effective approach to VLLM membership inference.
items.authors: Damien Lo, Hong Kyu Lee, Ruixuan Liu, Li Xiong

items.title: HarnessTTT: Learn to Optimize Harness at Test-Time for Scientific Discovery
items.abstract: Scientific discovery with language models requires finding the best valid solution within a finite computational budget. We study how feedback from this search can improve the procedure used to conduct it. We introduce HarnessTTT, a test-time learning framework that trains a harness proposer while keeping the executor frozen. The proposer generates executable harnesses comprising system prompts, reusable skills, tools, middleware, and execution controls. Each harness guides a budgeted discovery rollout, whose outcome provides feedback for updating the proposer. A discovery-oriented policy-gradient objective combines gap-normalized rewards, leave-one-out advantages (RLOO), and max-sharpening to favor high-performing proposals. Generated components are validated before execution, and the search retains the best valid solution and selected harnesses across rounds. Across fourteen discovery tasks in mathematics, systems, GPU kernels, heuristic programming, astrodynamics, and biology, HarnessTTT with a frozen 9B executor improves on OpenEvolve with the same executor on all eleven benchmark tasks (e.g., from 1.17 to 2.64 on circle packing), improves on the discovery-fine-tuned Finch-9B by up to 92%, holds the best open-weight sub-10B result on nine, and reaches 0.380919 on Erd\H{o}s minimum overlap, better than the best human reference of 0.380927. Scaling the proposer and frozen executor to 27B improves on eleven of fourteen tasks, and transferring the learned harnesses to GPT-5.5 matches or exceeds the strongest reported system of any backbone on nine of fourteen tasks. Together, these results show that harness search can itself be learned at test time: a trained proposer lets a small frozen executor search effectively, and the harnesses it finds carry over to stronger executors.
items.authors: Yingzi Ma, Yulong Cao, Nanxi Li, Fang Wu, Yizhe Zhang, James Zou, Yejin Choi, Chaowei Xiao

items.title: Robustly Reliable Learning for Regression
items.abstract: We introduce the problem of robustly reliable learning for the regression setting in adversarial environments. Given a test point $x_{test}$, a training dataset $S$ of $n$ data points, a corruption budget $b \ll n$, and a real-valued hypothesis class $\mathcal H$, our goal is to output the optimal prediction range $I^*_{x_{test}}(S, b)$, such that any $L$-Lipschitz predictor consistent with all but at most $b$ points in $S$ must predict a value $h(x_{test}) \in I$. We then instantiate the analysis for $L$-Lipschitz hypothesis classes, a natural and widely studied class in the regression setting, focusing on two key scenarios. First, for the restricted case where the corrupted dataset is guaranteed to be $L$-Lipschitz consistent, we propose a simple and efficient $b^{th}$-best heuristic algorithm and prove its correctness in computing the tightest possible range $I^*_{x_{test}}(S, b)$. We then establish its computational complexity of $O(n)$ and show that it is computationally optimal in this scenario. Building on this foundation, we address the general scenario where the dataset $S$ is no longer $L$-Lipschitz consistent. We demonstrate that computing the optimal range in this setting reduces to analyzing a violation graph, which models the pairwise $L$-Lipschitz violations among data points. By leveraging the structural properties of this graph's kernel, we propose a Fixed-Parameter Tractable (FPT) algorithm that computes the exact optimal range in $O(n^2 + b^4)$ time. Furthermore, under the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH), we establish a computational lower bound of $\Omega(n^{2 - o(1)})$, proving that our algorithm is computationally optimal. Finally, we discuss open directions for the problem of robustly reliable learning for regression.
items.authors: Avrim Blum, Anh Tuan Nguyen

items.title: Variable Input Masked Autoencoders for Wrist-Worn Accelerometry
items.abstract: Large-scale repositories of wearable sensor data have enabled the development of foundation models for human activities and behavior. However, existing models are pretrained using fixed input durations and sampling rates, despite substantial heterogeneity in recording conditions, downstream tasks, and deployment constraints. We introduce VarMAE, a variable input masked autoencoder that learns a single representation across sampling rates and temporal contexts. During pretraining we construct two views of the same signal: a long duration high frequency view, and a short duration lower frequency view, obtained via random cropping and downsampling. We perform masked reconstruction within each view and introduce a cross-resolution masked reconstruction objective that uses visible tokens from the long view to predict masked tokens from the short view. Cropping and downsampling impose complementary information bottlenecks, encouraging the model to learn representations that remain effective across input durations and sampling rate changes. We pretrain VarMAE on the large-scale NHANES dataset, producing a single pretrained encoder matching or outperforming controlled foundation model baselines on eight benchmark datasets. With only 3.82M parameters, VarMAE is parameter efficient and shows that a single foundation model can achieve broad transfer capabilities across sensing configurations.
items.authors: Harish Haresamudram, Wanting Mao, Aditya Radhakrishnan, Maxwell A. Xu, James M. Rehg

items.title: Measure Neural Mappings
items.abstract: We introduce and define measure neural mappings (MNMs), which combine measure-dependent neural transport with ensemble consistency for learning operators on probability measures. Ensemble consistency requires outputs from growing ensembles sampled from an input law to converge to the specified population output in probability. We establish quantitative continuum limits for attention on noncompact laws under strong sub-Gaussian and tail-integrability assumptions. These laws accommodate unbounded state spaces in scientific machine learning, including Bayesian inference and uncertainty quantification. For fixed self-attention transformers, the expected output Wasserstein error is bounded by the empirical input Wasserstein error plus an additional $N^{-1/2}$ attention term. These self-attention transformers are MNMs under the stated assumptions: pre-norm architectures follow from compact stability after normalization, while post-norm architectures are covered under the stated tail conditions. We prove corresponding cross-attention estimates and extend the results to multihead attention and grouped transformer evaluation, with convergence as the group size grows. For Set Transformers viewed as measure-to-vector mappings, we obtain an $N^{-1/2}$ bound on the expected Euclidean output error under the stated assumptions. Experiments on seven operators in dimensions $d=1,2,3,5,10$ support the predicted particle-count dependence, using one-dimensional Wasserstein computations and Sinkhorn approximations in higher dimensions. The observed Wasserstein and sliced Wasserstein decay rates are close to their respective theoretical sampling benchmarks.
items.authors: Ricardo Baptista, Edoardo Calvello, Bohan Chen, Andrew Stuart, Urbain Vaes

items.title: JustOPD: On-Policy Distillation from Autoregressive to Diffusion Language Models
items.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a post-training approach for large language models (LLMs) that enables a student model to learn a teacher model's distribution from sequences sampled from the student's own policy. Despite its promising capability, OPD for diffusion language models (DLMs) remains underexplored and existing studies primarily focuses on DLM-to-DLM distillation. The limited availability of strong teacher DLMs and the flexible generation order of DLMs impose additional technical challenges as well. However, it remains unclear how to effectively distill knowledge from a strong autoregressive language model (ARM) into a weaker DLM, given the mismatch between the left-to-right decoding of ARMs and the flexible decoding order of DLMs. Inspired by Ni et al. (2026), we propose JustOPD, an ARM-to-DLM on-policy distillation method that uses autoregressive rollouts during training to align the student's generation process with the ARM teacher's left-to-right decoding. This alignment enables effective distillation from ARM teachers while preserving the DLM's flexible generation-order capability at inference time. Experiments using Qwen3-14B as the teacher and Dream-7B as the student demonstrate that JustOPD consistently improves mathematical reasoning performance over the base DLM across multiple divergence choices.
items.authors: Zikun Zhang, Jiayuan Sheng, David D. Yao, Wenpin Tang

items.title: Position: Beyond Training Time, Test-Time Coordination is Essential for Cooperative MARL
items.abstract: We argue that cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) should treat test-time coordination as part of the problem definition rather than a deployment artifact. Our focus is on long-horizon, centrally monitored cooperative systems such as warehouse robotics, automated storage-and-retrieval systems, and cloud-resource scheduling, where teams share a reward, operate under shifting objectives, and already run with global telemetry at deployment. The dominant paradigm in this regime, centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE), uses global information only during training and provides no coordination channel at execution. This is sufficient when agents are weakly coupled or the environment is stationary, but it fails when the team must realign after conditions change. The limitation is structural rather than algorithmic, and more training cannot add a channel that does not exist at execution time. We call this the recoverability gap. To address it, we name the underexplored design space of intermittent test-time coordination as centralized training with mixed execution (CTME), in which a coordinator observes global state and emits high-level signals while agents act locally. CTME is not a particular learning algorithm, but a cooperative MARL problem setting that makes test-time information structure explicit. It specifies team-level information, high-level signals, and update frequency after training, with CTDE recovered as a limit case. We do not argue that CTDE is obsolete. We argue that removing the test-time channel is a modeling choice, not a necessity, and the wrong default when global telemetry is available and teams must recover from drift.
items.authors: Dongsu Lee, Sooraj Sathish, Joonkyung Kim, Woojun Kim, Amy Zhang

items.title: When Sparsity Breaks Connectivity: Functional Reachability and Guided Topology Dynamics in Extreme Sparse Training
items.abstract: Dynamic Sparse Training (DST) periodically prunes and regrows connections, inducing a discrete dynamical mechanism over network topologies. At extreme sparsity ($\ge 99\%$), this dynamic tends to destroy input-output information pathways, and performance with standard magnitude/random updates degrades sharply. We formalize forward, backward, and functional reachability on layered sparse graphs, derive closed-form expectations for reachable neurons and edges, and show that Monte Carlo realizations match the theory. Guided by this reachability-based structure, we bias pruning toward non-functional edges and regrowth toward functionally consistent candidates. We introduce this reachability-driven modification of topology evolution as Reachability-guided in DST, referred to as guided DST. On CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny ImageNet, guided DST recovers large accuracy gaps versus unguided DST (up to $+14.4$ points at $99.9\%$ sparsity on CIFAR-100), and on MLP-Mixer guided DST remains trainable at $99.99\%$ sparsity while unguided random regrowth degrades sharply. These results cast extreme-sparse training as a connectivity-preserving dynamical process. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/mzjaworski/ea_dst.
items.authors: Mohammad Pasande, Mateusz Jaworski, Jeroen Rook, Elena Mocanu

items.title: Monarch-Muon: Structure-Aware Muon for Fast and Memory-Efficient Pretraining
items.abstract: Training large language models is constrained by both wall-clock time and memory footprint, and recent matrix-aware optimizers sharpen this tradeoff: Muon can improve optimization but its dense polar update remains expensive. We propose Monarch-Muon, a structured matrix-aware optimizer for weights parameterized by Monarch factors. The resulting structure reduces weights, gradients, and optimizer state, and exposes small independent update subproblems in place of a single dense orthogonalization; we formalize this through a blockwise trust-region interpretation. In quality runs, Monarch-Muon improves over Monarch-AdamW at fixed structure: 3.06 vs. 3.09 in the dense 257M model and 2.68 vs. 2.77 in the 1B MoE model; the two-block MoE variant also matches dense AdamW while using 15% fewer active and 25.4% fewer total parameters. In 6.89B-parameter systems measurements, Monarch-Muon reduces peak memory from 68.9 to 52.9 GB, Muon optimizer state from 14.60 to 6.77 GB, and the Muon optimizer step from 1288 to 304 ms.
items.authors: Alexander Miasnikov, Ruslan Kabirov, Gleb Molodtsov, Dmitrii Vlashchuk, Vladimir Aletov, Nail Bashirov, Daniil Tikhonov, Maxim Krutikov, Aleksandr Shestakov, Aleksandr Beznosikov

items.title: On Sleep-Wake Disorder Identification from Polysomnographic Representations
items.abstract: Self-supervised polysomnography foundation models (PSG FMs) aim to capture clinically useful information beyond sleep staging, yet are rarely compared with sleep-staging encoders pretrained at comparable scale and modality coverage. Using a common whole-night, missingness-aware state-space downstream modeling framework, we compared frozen representations from prominent large-scale, multi-cohort sleep-stage-supervised encoders and self-supervised PSG FMs for multilabel identification of six sleep-wake and circadian disorder groups in 7,906 PSGs from an unseen registry. Although PSG FMs outperformed an EEG-only, single-cohort supervised baseline, this ordering reversed when supervised pretraining approached comparable scale and modality coverage. Transfer learning from neural sleep scorers achieved higher overall performance while exhibiting greater downstream data efficiency. These findings underscore the need for scale- and modality-matched pretrained supervised baselines when assessing PSG FMs' downstream potential.
items.authors: Alvise Dei Rossi, Luigi Fiorillo, Giuliana Monachino, Alessia Calzoni, Julia van der Meer, Markus H. Schmidt, Claudio L. A. Bassetti, Silvia Santini, Francesca Faraci

items.title: Effect of Spherical Parameter Space on Number of Non-Forgetting Tasks and Capacity of Continual Learning
items.abstract: We propose a continuous learning formulation for $T$ non-forgetting tasks with the spherical parameter space $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}(\sqrt{d})$ in asymptotic regime $d\rightarrow \infty$. Each task $i$ has an optimum $\bm{\Theta}_i$, minimizing its corresponding loss function $R_i(\bm{w})$ on sphere. We reduce each task $i$ to an acceptable loss region modeled by a geodesic ball $B_{\bm{\Theta}_i}(r_i(d))$ on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}(\sqrt{d})$ centered at $\bm{\Theta}_i$ with radius $r_i(d)$. To model task dependencies (similarities), task optima $\bm{\Theta}_i$ are distributed by a Neyman-Scott clustered point process $\Phi$. Cluster centers $\{\bm{Y}_j\}_{j=1}^{N_p}$ form a homogeneous Poisson point process on sphere, while intra-cluster task optima follow a von Mises-Fisher distribution with mean $\bm{Y}_j$ and concentration $\kappa$. Each task $t\in \{1, ..., T\}$ learning algorithm is considered to be a channel $Q_{t}(\mathrm{d}\bm{w}_t | \bm{w}_{t-1}, \mathcal{K}_{t-1}(\bm{\theta}_{1:t-1}), \bm{\theta}_t)$, where $\bm{W}_t$ is the learned parameter of task $t$ and $\mathcal{K}_{t-1}(\bm{\Theta}_{1:t-1})=\bigcap_{i=1}^{t-1}B_{\bm{\Theta}_i}(r_i(d))$. Since in continual learning, the learner does not need to reach $\bm{\Theta}_t$ exactly to successfully learn task $t$, to avoid forgetting as well as reliable learning, it only needs for the learned parameter vector $\bm{W}_{t}$ to enter $B_{\bm{\Theta}_t}(r_t(d)) \cap \mathcal{K}_{t-1}(\bm{\Theta}_{1:t-1})$. Using this model, we derive an upper bound on $T$ ensuring $\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{K}_{T}(\bm{\Theta}_{1:T}) \neq \emptyset] \rightarrow 1$ as $d\rightarrow \infty$ and $\kappa/d \rightarrow \alpha$, where $\alpha>0$ is a constant. Finally, for $T$ tasks sampled uniformly from $\Phi$, we derive an upper bound for total information theoretic capacity under the non-forgetting constraint for each task.
items.authors: Nazanin Mirhosseini

items.title: Structure-preserving fidelity diagnostics for partial differential equations
items.abstract: Machine learning surrogates of partial differential equations (PDEs) are commonly trained on data generated by numerical solvers. Therefore, the training data obey not the PDE but the modified equation of the numerical scheme, and the test loss, computed on data from the same solver, cannot distinguish a model that learned the physics from one that learned the discretization error. Here, we show that the difference is nevertheless visible in the trained model. We propose a suite of structure-preserving fidelity diagnostics, simple scores that measure whether a learned model respects one known property of the physics, such as a conserved quantity, a symmetry or a Hamiltonian structure, without access to the training data or the governing equation. Over five systems, the diagnostics track the error with respect to the true dynamics with a rank correlation of up to $0.94$, while the test loss is uncorrelated or anti-correlated with it. For the Burgers, Korteweg-de Vries and Navier-Stokes equations, the diagnostics separate numerical schemes that the test loss ranks as equivalent, including schemes of the same order. order.
items.authors: Kyriakos Flouris

items.title: A Time-Synchronous Prequential Evaluation Framework for Next-Week Student Disengagement Prediction from Moodle LMS Logs
items.abstract: Retrospective evaluation of early-warning models may not reflect information available when predictions are issued and outcomes become observable. We developed a time-synchronous prequential framework for online prediction of next-week student disengagement, operationalised as inactivity onset, from Moodle logs. Ordered by calendar time, models were updated only with available outcomes and remained unchanged for all predictions at each prediction cutoff; development, calibration and evaluation were chronologically separate. We compared stochastic gradient descent logistic regression (SGD-LR), online sequential extreme learning machine (OSELM) and echo state network (ESN) across predictive performance, fixed, frozen and rolling threshold policies, calendar-time variation and four behavioural feature sets. Held-out evaluation comprised 49,329 predictions with 37.68% inactivity-onset prevalence. Discrimination was similar (average precision 0.665-0.679; ROC-AUC 0.755-0.774). OSELM had the highest recall, SGD-LR the highest precision and specificity, and ESN the highest Matthews correlation coefficient and balanced accuracy. Lower thresholds increased recall and alert volume, whereas rolling adaptation did not improve MCC over frozen thresholds. Weekly performance and calibrated-probability distributions varied without sustained deterioration. During model selection, cumulative-and-temporal features achieved the highest individual-set AP, with modest gains from combining all feature groups. These findings indicate that streaming early-warning evaluation should consider calibration, threshold-dependent performance, alert burden and calendar-time variation alongside aggregate discrimination.
items.authors: David Otoo-Arthur, Terence L. van Zyl

items.title: Longitudinal Learner Participation Profiling in Online Learning: Heterogeneous Consensus Clustering under Unequal Observation Windows
items.abstract: Learning management system traces are clustered to identify participation profiles, but unequal observation windows may cause profiles to reflect duration rather than participation alone. Using 16,448 complete learner--course sequences from 4,599 learners across 152 courses at a South African public university, we evaluated eight participation measures. All remained related to observation-window length even when expressed as rates or shares. Course-grouped adjustment reduced these relationships. Five retained measures were evaluated using K-means, Gaussian mixtures, Ward agglomerative clustering and K-medoids, with standardised measures and principal-component summaries. Evidence supported a broad two-profile grouping and a more detailed adjusted four-profile consensus: Gradually declining, Early-concentrated, Cyclical variable and Sustained active. Profile membership accounted for 2.87% of the variation in duration in the primary consensus, versus 38.18% using original measures. Mean assignment support was 0.739; 8.35% of assignments fell below 0.50, with greatest uncertainty in Sustained active. Two week-by-week sequence analyses agreed strongly with each other but only modestly with the four-profile consensus, indicating that the profiles combined multiple aspects of participation rather than distinct sequence patterns. Profiling should therefore assess duration effects, compare clustering methods and participation summaries, and report assignment consistency.
items.authors: David Otoo-Arthur, Terence L. van Zyl

items.title: A Sense of Proprioception in Language Models
items.abstract: In humans, proprioception corresponds to the sense of self-movement or position, e.g. understanding the position of one's arm. This sense is often less well-understood and in popular understanding sometimes conflated with introspection. But, notably, proprioception is a separate sense, with dedicated receptors and verifiable outcomes. On the other hand though, language models cannot observe their own internal states during training (and for example answer the question which experts activated in a certain layer of an MoE) and so cannot accurately report on them. Yet, such information is, by virtue of being internal to the model, both accessible, and readily constructed into verifiable signals. We argue that this provides the basis for a digital analog of proprioception. As such, we train models through SFT and on-policy training to equip them with this ability. We show that modern models can be trained to understand a range of subtypes of proprioception, such as routing decision awareness, token entropy, decision depth or logit lens information, without affecting model capabilities. We then run these models through a broad evaluation of situational awareness, legibility, and epiphenomenality, to evaluate in what ways access to proprioception changes model behavior.
items.authors: Jonas Geiping

items.title: Merit: Making every modality earn its contribution in multimodal attention decoding
items.abstract: More than 1.5 billion people have hearing loss. When several people talk at once, hearing aids amplify every voice alike. Auditory attention decoding (AAD) aims to solve this by reading a listener's brain signals to find the attended talker, letting the device amplify only them. A real device will not see the brain alone; smart glasses and earbuds also track eyes, head, and scene. These behavioral signals help, as people often look at who they listen to. However, they show where a listener looks, not whom they hear. A decoder relying heavily on them fails when a listener cannot move their head or listens without looking - exactly when a brain-based device is needed. A multimodal decoder must use these signals without letting them replace the electroencephalogram (EEG). Accuracy alone cannot show whether it does. We present MERIT, a decoder and evaluation method asking: how much accuracy does each input earn? MERIT shuffles each input stream across test examples, measures the accuracy drop, and splits the result across streams using Shapley values. It also blocks two shortcuts: candidate audio is checked before training so it cannot reveal the answer, and the scoring function cannot beat chance if it ignores the brain. On a public dataset with EEG, eye tracking, head motion, and scene video, MERIT improves on the published benchmark, reaching 0.82 four-way accuracy within listeners and 0.74 on unseen listeners (chance is 0.25). The measurement reveals what accuracy hides: adding behavioral streams raises overall accuracy but almost halves the brain's share of it. On two other datasets, the same tests find a label imbalance in a widely used benchmark and flag results that accuracy alone would report as brain decoding.
items.authors: Ali Alavi, Donald S. Williamson

items.title: C{\AE}NL: Collapse-Based Active Neural Learning with Objective-Aligned Representation Control
items.abstract: Active learning changes the representations used to acquire subsequent labels. We study this interaction through Collapse-Based Active Neural Learning (C{\AE}NL), which separates acquisition, Dynamic Collapse Regularization (DCR), and its coefficient policy. DCR penalizes a normalized within-class to between-class scatter residual above a frozen reference, with a separate class-separation safeguard. Fixed, scheduled, deterministic-feedback, and learned-feedback policies apply this objective. The analysis establishes scatter invariances, conditional local descent, and coefficient bounds, and shows why clean geometry alone cannot guarantee input robustness. Six-seed classification comparisons are complemented by a 104-run study with separate control selection and ten-seed evaluations on each of two backbones. At 60% annotations on ImageNet-100, entropy acquisition with DCR and MACC-Lite reaches 73.420 +/- 0.512% accuracy on ResNet-50 and 73.086 +/- 0.397% on ResNet-18 (mean +/- seed SD), exceeding entropy alone by 1.742 and 1.834 percentage points. Both gains survive Holm correction under paired-t and exact sign-flip tests, with unchanged feedback settings across backbones. Independently tuned constants attain slightly higher mean accuracy; the paired comparisons establish neither adaptive superiority nor equivalence. Separate six-seed spectral studies yield a small fixed-regularization C4 loss reduction, worse CIFAR-10 diffusion FID, and inconclusive AudioCaps captioning effects. Earlier classification studies find near-zero AutoAttack accuracy at L-infinity radius 8/255 and no added benefit from learned control. The results support the evaluated combined classification treatment and identify the task dependence of geometry-informed regularization.
items.authors: Saad Alqithami

items.title: FedLoRD: Personalized Federated Learning based on Low-Rank Structures of Model Parameter Differences
items.abstract: We propose FedLoRD, a personalized federated learning (PFL) method based on the low-rank structure of the differences between the global and personalized model parameters. PFL is a branch of federated learning that aims to learn models tailored to the local data of each client under biased local data distributions. In its local training, each client learns a personalized model by regularizing the difference between its model parameters and the global ones sent from the server. The regularization function needs to be designed with priors on the model parameter difference; however, the existing PFL methods rely on empirical choices (e.g., $\ell_1$- and $\ell_2$-norms), which do not take into account the actual characteristics of the difference. The resulting mismatch of priors can lead to suboptimal personalized models. To address this issue, we propose a PFL method whose regularizer is built on an observed characteristic of the model parameter differences: they are approximately low-rank at every layer. In our method, we first formulate a local training problem with nuclear norm regularization on the layer-wise differences. We further rewrite this problem via the factorized representation of the nuclear norm so that it can be efficiently solved by a plain stochastic gradient descent method. Image classification experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that FedLoRD outperforms several existing PFL methods.
items.authors: Tsutahiro Fukuhara, Junya Hara, Hiroshi Higashi, Yuichi Tanaka

items.title: Calibrated Disambiguation for Partial Multi-label Learning
items.abstract: Partial multi-label learning (PML) aims to train a classifier on datasets whose instances are over-annotated with not only relevant labels but also irrelevant labels, which is common when datasets are collected from crowd-sourcing platform. Existing works primarily approach it from a curriculum learning perspective, leveraging the memorization effect to disambiguate noisy labels and produce robust predictions. However, these methods are based on non-adaptive weighting functions and lack theoretical guidance for optimal weighting. To overcome these issues, a calibrated disambiguation model named PML-CD is proposed. We first formulate the optimal weighting function for curriculum-based disambiguation, which is equivalent to the calibration of the model's predicted confidences, thus providing guidance for curriculum designing. To obtain the optimal weighting function from PML dataset during the training, a transferable calibrator is designed, which takes the histogram of positive samples' confidences as input, and outputs the optimal curriculum weighting for training. Prototype alignment regularization is also proposed to promote the model's performance. Experiments conducted on Pascal VOC, MS-COCO, NUS-WIDE and CUB have verified that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art PML methods.
items.authors: Zhuoming Li, Yuheng Jia, Mi Yu, Zicong Miao

items.title: Mixed Precision Scaling Laws for Quantized Pretraining
items.abstract: Since scaling laws were introduced for modern LLMs (Kaplan et al., 2020), several works have extended them to account for quantization, tracking the emerging low-precision data types supported on AI accelerators. We develop a more accurate scaling law for quantized pretraining with mixed precision across the forward and backward passes, grounded in optimization theory and validated empirically. Our formulation separates the effects of quantization on model capacity and on optimization efficiency, and explicitly models the persistent optimization error from forward and backward quantization identified through convergence analysis. To select the regimes for fitting and evaluating our law, we first decompose existing 4-bit training recipes into their forward and backward components, isolating those that most affect loss. Our Qwen3 experiments under selected 4-bit regimes, together with published Llama-style experiments, show that our law predicts loss with up to $11\times$ lower MSE than existing laws as model size and token count scale. Finally, we extend our law to layer-wise mixed precision and identify the optimal quantized-pretraining recipe, i.e., model size, training tokens, and per-layer forward/backward precision, under a hardware-aware compute budget. Unlike prior precision scaling laws, our law predicts that the optimal precision increases with the compute budget.
items.authors: Jinuk Kim, Rajarshi Saha, Muhammed Fatih Balin, Youngsuk Park

items.title: DisaggKD: Efficient Knowledge Distillation through Teacher-Student Disaggregation and a Fused Loss
items.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) frameworks place teacher and student on the same GPUs, so per-GPU memory limits the teachers that fit. DisaggKD separates them across nodes: teacher replicas stream hidden states to the student, a KD loss over row windows and vocabulary shards equals the full-vocabulary loss in exact arithmetic without forming the full-vocabulary logits, and a prefetch ring paces producer and trainer. Closed-form memory and traffic models locate the memory limits of each layout. On the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B to 9B pair, the disaggregated layout matches the LM loss of the colocated run with the same loss and is faster than that run; our fused loss also lets a colocated run train on as few nodes at faster speed, while the split is memory efficient when the student spans several nodes. On the larger pairs, colocated runs with a fused loss still run OOM where the split trains, because teacher weights and student states fill the budget.
items.authors: Ruixuan Tu, Yuyang Dong

items.title: Focus on What You Need: Global-to-Local Dynamic Attention for Multimodal Sarcasm Detection
items.abstract: Multimodal sarcasm detection has attracted increasing attention due to the widespread use of images and text on social media platforms. Existing studies generally treat the semantic or emotional inconsistency between images and text as a key cue for identifying sarcastic expressions. However, images in real-world scenarios often contain multiple visual objects, many of which are irrelevant to sarcasm-related semantics. Such redundant visual information may introduce noise during cross-modal interaction, distracting models from focusing on critical sarcasm cues and potentially leading to inaccurate predictions. To address this issue, we propose GLDA (Global-to-Local Dynamic Attention), a multimodal sarcasm detection framework that models cross-modal interactions from a global-to-local perspective. Specifically, GLDA first employs a global multimodal fusion module to capture high-level semantic interactions between visual and textual modalities, enabling the model to identify coarse-grained cross-modal inconsistencies. To further reduce the influence of irrelevant objects, GLDA introduces a local gated cross-modal attention mechanism that dynamically filters redundant visual and textual features and refines multimodal representations at a finer granularity. In addition, a multi-branch learning objective is designed to jointly optimize unimodal and multimodal representations. Experimental results demonstrate that GLDA effectively improves sarcasm detection performance and achieves competitive results compared with existing approaches. The code will be available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/GLDA-DBE6.
items.authors: Dehao Wu, Xingjie Zhuang

items.title: Confine to the Task, Anchor the Rest: Concept-Guided Retention Regularizer for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
items.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has been widely used, yet the adapted model suffers catastrophic forgetting of pre-trained knowledge. While most existing work hardens the adapter by constraining where the weight update may lie, we note that constraining this weight channel does not constrain the activation channel. In this paper, we propose Concept-Guided Retention (CGR), a plug-and-play regularizer that constrains both for any PEFT base. CGR reads a frozen sparse autoencoder (SAE) and treats two disjoint concept sets differently. It softly confines the update to the task-concept subspace (via weight channel), and anchors a selected set of general-purpose concepts to the frozen model (via activation channel). We also provide anchor value bounds based on weight updates to understand how they interact, and show that both terms are necessary. On a CLIP vision panel, CGR significantly improves retention at comparable accuracy for every base, and the same pattern holds for world-knowledge retention under Llama-3.1-8B instruction tuning. Because the protected directions are named SAE concepts, CGR remains inspectable and controllable.
items.authors: Ibna Kowsar, Ivan Medri, Fanyu Meng, Xin Liu

items.title: MissPath-FM: Flow Matching with Structured Priors for Partially Observed Time Series
items.abstract: Flow matching has emerged as a powerful alternative to diffusion models for generative modeling, but standard conditional flow matching is fundamentally misaligned with partially observed time series: starting from an uninformed Gaussian source forces the model to transport even already-observed entries from noise to the target, wasting capacity on trivially known regions. We propose MissPath-FM, a partial-observation-aware flow matching framework that redesigns the source prior and probability path for incomplete time series. MissPath-FM employs structured source priors (interpolation priors and Gaussian process posterior priors) to initialize the flow close to the observed signal, paired with a missingness-aware smooth path that allocates transport asymmetrically between observed and missing regions. We evaluate systematically across four datasets, four missingness mechanisms (MCAR, block, MNAR, irregular), two missing ratios, and three sequence lengths (T in {24, 48, 96}), totaling 48 settings against eight baselines. MissPath-FM wins 29 of 32 settings at T=48 and 45 of 48 overall (93.8%). Our ablations reveal a regime-dependent design hierarchy in which no single component suffices: under random missingness the source prior yields a large initial gain, but under structured block missingness it can fail entirely and the learned flow becomes indispensable; the missingness-aware path contributes a further 12%-26% across all regimes. Mechanistically, structured priors shorten observed-region transport by up to 15x, concentrating the velocity field on genuinely uncertain entries. Project page: https://zgp110.github.io/misspath-fm/
items.authors: Genpei Zhang

items.title: Hybrid Parallel Bessel KAN Model: a Kolmogorov Arnold Network: integrated framework for developing a novel architecture to reconstruct the fused-basis approach via a parameter free quadratic interaction
items.abstract: The Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (KAN) challenges traditional MLPs by placing learnable activation functions on network edges. However, scaling KANs to spatial data exposes limitations in default B-Splines. While hybrid architectures mix multiple basis families on a single edge to resolve this, monolithic superposition causes geometric overlap, parameter explosion, and severe numerical ill-conditioning ($\kappa(G) \approx 10^{16}$).To overcome this, we propose Parallel BesselKAN, which isolates B-Spline and low-order Bessel branches into parallel processing pipelines integrated via a parameter-free quadratic interaction. This decoupled architecture acts as an efficient internal ensemble, bypassing monolithic stability bottlenecks. It compresses the parameter footprint by $35\%$ while achieving $97.99\%$ accuracy on MNIST. Although standard MLPs retain a hardware speed advantage for pure vision tasks, Parallel BesselKAN provides a robust, parameter-efficient framework stabilizing mixed-basis networks and paving the way for scalable spatial adaptations like Convolutional KANs.
items.authors: Mintu Pathak, Meshv Patel, Mohendra Roy, Jwngsar Brahma

items.title: Follow the Perturbed Leader for Linear Bandits: $\sqrt{T}$ Regret over General Convex Sets
items.abstract: We give the first adversarial linear bandit algorithm based on Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader (FTPL) that achieves $\sqrt{T}$ regret over general convex action sets. Our algorithm attains $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(d^{5/4}\sqrt{T})$ regret using only linear optimization oracles, and the near-optimal $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(d\sqrt{T})$ regret when an optimal-design exploration distribution is further available. This improves on the $T^{2/3}$ regret of the FTPL algorithm of Dani and Hayes (2006) for general convex sets, and generalizes the $\sqrt{T}$ regret of L\'evy et al. (2026) over two special action sets (hypercube and Euclidean ball). Compared to previous oracle-efficient linear bandit algorithms based on continuous exponential weights, the FTPL approach generally has better computational efficiency, and is much simpler to implement. The key algorithmic element is a perturbation distribution that adapts to the estimated rewards. Its simplest form, an adaptive Gaussian perturbation, is straightforward to implement and already attains the regret bound above. We further extend it to two general constructions, random-weighting and elliptical perturbations, each covering distributions from light tails (Gaussian) to heavy tails (Student-$t_2$). On the technical side, we develop a systematic way to analyze the stability term in the FTPL regret through the Fisher information of the perturbation distribution. This builds a general framework for FTPL beyond existing ones such as the hazard rate and the FTRL-FTPL duality.
items.authors: Chen-Yu Wei

items.title: GeoNIRS: Geometry-Aware Pretraining for Heterogeneous fNIRS Representation Learning
items.abstract: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) provides portable and spatially localized measurements of cortical hemodynamics, but differences in channel count, probe layout, signal distribution, and task type hinder joint pretraining across datasets. We introduce GeoNIRS, a geometry-aware framework that uses source-detector locations as a shared spatial reference across heterogeneous probe layouts. GeoNIRS compresses variable-size channel sets into a fixed-size latent representation and employs bidirectional HbO/HbR cross-reconstruction with contiguous temporal masking. GeoNIRS-base is pretrained on eight heterogeneous datasets, while GeoNIRS-large scales to 22 datasets. Neither downstream data nor labels are used during pretraining, enabling evaluation under a strict cross-task setting. To our knowledge, GeoNIRS is the first fNIRS framework to explicitly model physical channel geometry during joint pretraining across heterogeneous channel configurations, and the first to provide complete source code and downloadable pretrained checkpoints. We evaluate GeoNIRS on eight held-out tasks spanning clinical and auditory assessment, pain and affective processing, semantic decoding, and motor function. GeoNIRS achieves the highest task-averaged balanced accuracy among the evaluated conventional machine-learning, fNIRS-specific, general time-series, and fNIRS pretraining baselines. Compared with random initialization, pretraining improves average balanced accuracy by 4.12 percentage points under linear probing and 3.30 points under full fine-tuning, with larger benefits when labels are scarce. GeoNIRS also remains robust to missing input channels. Geometry perturbations and pretraining ablations further show that both channel geometry and cross-chromophore reconstruction contribute to the learned representations.
items.authors: Zongsheng Li, Shengyuan Zhu, Zimo Zhang, Hanyao Li, Shengming Wang, Quanying Liu

items.title: Persistence Positional Encoding: A Minimal Transformer Recipe for Persistence Diagrams
items.abstract: Persistence diagrams (PDs) represent multiscale topological information as multisets of birth-death pairs $(b,d)$. How best to use them with Transformers, however, remains unclear. Connecting PDs to Transformers requires choosing how topological information is tokenized and exposed to self-attention. Prior methods use specialized designs for tokenization, aggregation, Transformer blocks, or attention, but are hard to compare since reported results rarely share PD inputs, splits, or model-selection rules. We instead confine the diagram-specific design to point representation, mapping each birth-death pair through fixed random Fourier features while leaving the Transformer backbone unchanged, and call this recipe Persistence Positional Encoding (PPE). In matched controls on eight TU graph benchmarks (TU8), changing only point representation shifts macro accuracy by 5.49 to 6.47 percentage points (pp), against 0.47 to 1.45 pp from changing the downstream module, identifying point representation as the dominant design variable tested. We further reevaluate vectorizations, kernels, learned representations, and Transformer-based models under one protocol with shared PD inputs, outer folds, and validation-only selection. Among all evaluated PD methods and downstream configurations, PPE achieves the highest mean on most benchmarks, including TU8, ORBIT5K, and MCB-C. Finally, we prove that grid averaging leaves a reconstruction error at any resolution, whereas a Transformer with fixed random Fourier frequencies is almost surely universal. PPE thus offers a minimal, Transformer-native baseline for persistence diagrams, and a common protocol for future comparison.
items.authors: Eunwoo Heo, Ganghyun Kim, Jaejun Yoo

items.title: Searching for What Matters: Open-Ended Discovery of Multiple Hypotheses with Agentic Data Exploration
items.abstract: Discovering what drives an outcome from data is central to science and often requires deciding what is worth investigating before a specific hypothesis is known. Yet most existing hypothesis generation settings substantially narrow this search by providing a research question, target relationship, or curated context. We introduce open-ended multiple hypothesis discovery, where a system receives only a large tabular dataset and an outcome and must discover multiple data-supported hypotheses without knowing in advance the relevant variables, functional forms, conditions, or number of underlying mechanisms. To study this problem, we introduce a benchmark built from structural causal models grounded in real-world data schemas, containing 351 planted hypotheses across 15 tasks and five domains, with 53--65 variables and 1M--10M rows per task. The causal model is hidden from the discovery method and retained only by the evaluator, allowing proposed hypotheses to be tested through interventions and separating observational discovery from causal validation. We further propose HypAgent, which treats the dataset as an interactive environment and performs iterative search by proposing candidate directions, triaging and refining promising hypotheses, and removing explained signal so that each accepted discovery redirects subsequent search. HypAgent achieves 0.47 precision, 0.51 recall, and 0.49 F1, compared with 0.35 F1 for the strongest baseline. Our analysis shows that many failures occur after a relevant variable has already been surfaced, suggesting that correctly characterizing a mechanism's functional form and conditions, rather than merely identifying relevant variables, remains a key challenge in open-ended discovery.
items.authors: Sanchit Kabra, Nurendra Choudhary, Jiangshu Du, Eddie Huang, Danai Koutra, Chandan K Reddy

items.title: Deep Mesoscopic Dynamics
items.abstract: Microscopic simulations resolve spatial patterns but are feasible only over small domains and short timescales, whereas bulk descriptions erase those patterns through spatial averaging. Mesoscopic fields preserve this spatial organisation, but their effective equations are known only for selected microscopic systems and scaling limits. We introduce Deep Mesoscopic Dynamics (DeepMesoD), which uses neural networks to learn an effective mesoscopic field equation from microscopic trajectories at a prescribed coarse-graining scale. For the nonconserved dissipative dynamics studied here, DeepMesoD learns the free-energy functional with a spatial interaction kernel and a state-dependent dissipation operator constrained by the fluctuation-dissipation relation. We first validate the construction in the Ising-Kac model, where the learned mesoscopic equation recovers the known hydrodynamic limit and rollouts remain stable far beyond the training horizon. We then treat two systems without closed-form mesoscopic descriptions. For a two-dimensional Heisenberg ferromagnet governed by atomistic spin dynamics, DeepMesoD learns a mesoscopic model whose predictions match atomistic references up to 1 ns, and a rollout with an unseen initial condition remains bounded up to 25 ns. For layered CrBr$_3$, the learned kernel captures the suppression and sign reversal of interlayer coupling at a stacking fault whose location and strength are not supplied as inputs. Controlled changes to the learned interaction show how fault number and placement shape multistep magnetic responses, complementing our magneto-photoluminescence measurements. Across the two atomistic systems, DeepMesoD achieves a three-to-four-order-of-magnitude reduction in wall-clock time compared with atomistic spin dynamics.
items.authors: Yue Zhao, Shiqi Wu, Yihang Ouyang, Sergey Grebenchuk, Magdalena Grzeszczyk, Xiaoxu Zhao, Kostya S. Novoselov, Maciej Koperski, Qianxiao Li

items.title: FlashMask-3: Efficient and Expressive Mask-Aware Distributed Attention
items.abstract: Long-context training of large language and multimodal models couples structured attention masks (document, prefix-LM, share-question, sliding-window, block-sparse) with multi-node context parallelism, making the mask a dominant bottleneck. FlashMask's column-wise sparse mask compresses them from $O(n^2)$ to $O(n)$ via four query-axis boundary vectors, covering broad structured patterns. Implemented for Ampere GPUs, it neither exploits FlashAttention-3's TMA/WGMMA warp-specialized pipeline on Hopper nor supports distribution. The column-wise sparse mask is indexed by key positions but stores query-axis interval boundaries. Under any multi-chunk context-parallel assignment, it reduces per-rank mask localization to a provably zero-communication \emph{clip--shift--max} on the boundary vectors, compatible with the single-GPU kernel. FlashMask-3 introduces a mask-aware Hopper kernel with three-role warp specialization atop FlashAttention-3's TMA/WGMMA pipeline, plus a mask-aware distributed extension: zero-communication mask localization, a sparsity-aware load balancer (HCC-IPO), and a mask-aware compute-communication overlap with mask-driven communication pruning, whose forward all-gather uses topology-aware hierarchical routing. On a single H100 across 12 masks at 4K--128K context, it improves achieved TFLOPs over FlashMask, FlexAttention, and MagiAttention by 45--141%, 34--71%, and 2--44%. At context-parallel degrees 4--32 with 8K sequence per device, it attains 31--75% compute-communication overlap efficiency and improves throughput over Megatron-Core CP ring, Megatron-Core CP all-gather, and MagiAttention by $1.80\times$--$3.71\times$, $1.71\times$--$2.92\times$, and $1.09\times$--$1.46\times$. In end-to-end training of a 118B-A14B MoE at 128K on 128 H100 GPUs, it raises throughput by 7.3--11.0% over a Dual Chunk all-gather baseline, with attention forward+backward 24.5--44.9% faster.
items.authors: Guoxia Wang, Qianyue He, Siming Wu, Haoyang Xie, Qiwen Bao, Jinle Zeng, Jiabin Yang, Tian Wu, Dianhai Yu

items.title: Stable-Plastic Subspace Construction for Differentially Private Continual LoRA
items.abstract: Continual learning (CL) adapts pretrained models to a sequence of tasks while retaining knowledge acquired from earlier tasks. When task data are sensitive, differential privacy (DP) provides record-level protection, but maintaining both adaptation and retention under privacy constraints remains challenging. We study this problem in continual low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and observe that: 1) private training increases forgetting primarily during subsequent adaptation rather than initial task acquisition; 2) jointly perturbing both LoRA factors introduces a non-negligible bilinear noise interaction; and 3) DP aggravates the stability-plasticity dilemma, hindering both knowledge retention and adaptation to new tasks. Based on these observations, we propose DP-SPA, which constructs a stable subspace from previously privatized updates and a plastic subspace from pretrained weights within its orthogonal complement. The method fixes these bases and privately optimizes only the LoRA factor, eliminating the bilinear noise interaction within each step. Before merging each task update, it rescales stable-direction coefficients using historical and current update energies. We establish a privacy guarantee and show that recalibration does not increase historical overlap and tightens a conditional upper bound on old-task loss increase. Experiments across five datasets, eight settings, and multiple privacy budgets show that DP-SPA improves average accuracy and reduces forgetting compared with the evaluated baselines.
items.authors: Jin Liu, Ning Xi, Yinbin Miao, Junkang Liu, Ke Cheng, Jianfeng Ma

items.title: NBCLT: Parameter-Agnostic Norm-Ball Clipped Local Training
items.abstract: Distributed learning with multiple local steps reduces communication but aggravates drift, and its practical performance often depends on carefully tuned hyperparameters under heterogeneous data and communication constraints. At the same time, recent Muon-type optimizers suggest that constraining updates within suitable norm balls provides a simple way to encode geometric priors into optimization. In this work, we propose NBCLT (Norm-Ball Clipped Local Training), a unified local-training framework for both federated learning (FL) and decentralized learning (DL). NBCLT combines a predict-and-correct local update rule with Euclidean projections onto flexible norm balls, thereby performing norm-ball clipping under flexible update geometries while retaining a simple implementation. In FL, its problem-parameter-free regime achieves $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$ communication complexity and $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-4})$ total stochastic-gradient complexity without assuming bounded heterogeneity, when the per-round local-computation budget is scaled appropriately with the horizon. In DL, NBCLT is compatible with both static and time-varying mixing and preserves these accuracy exponents under the analogous computation scaling, up to fixed network constants and an additive initialization cost.
items.authors: Linxuan Pan, Shucheng Yang, Junchi Yang

items.title: Stein Variational Distributional Reinforcement Learning: Score-Guided Particles for Multivariate Return Distributions
items.abstract: Decisions that weigh several reward signals against each other require the joint distribution of the return vector. Categorical critics scale exponentially in the reward dimension, and quantiles have no canonical multivariate analogue. Multivariate distributional critics therefore represent each return distribution by M equal-weight particles trained with a discrepancy loss. Beyond their atoms, the particles provide no sampler and cannot resolve events rarer than 1/M. We propose Stein variational distributional RL (SVDRL). Its critic outputs Stein particles, which Stein variational gradient descent transports along a learned score field of the distributional Bellman target. We learn this field by bootstrapped denoising score matching across noise levels and tie it across the Bellman recursion by a consistency loss, which we prove is a non-expansive temporal-difference scheme in score space. The same field certifies the particles. Its reverse-diffusion sampler satisfies a supremal Wasserstein policy-evaluation bound that holds for bounded, possibly multimodal returns. The Stein particles inherit this bound up to a gap that we measure without ground truth, and the sampler answers tail-risk queries below the particle resolution at any sample size. Empirically, SVDRL is more accurate on rare events than particle critics with the same number of particles, and on par on MuJoCo continuous control.
items.authors: Manuel Hau{\ss}mann, Melih Kandemir
