The conservative update can leave much of the interaction between the intercept and the coefficients unresolved, producing a slowdown when that interaction controls convergence. A single Newton step avoids this attenuation and, in our experiments, follows nearly the same outer trajectory as exact minimization while requiring fewer inner steps. Simulated and real-data experiments, including comparisons across six production solvers and a controlled intervention within skglm, support this explanation. We also show how the same mechanism appears in quadratic-approximation methods and extends to multinomial models with rare classes. We recommend a safeguarded Newton update for direct coordinate descent and full intercept optimization within frozen local quadratic surrogates.
items.authors: Johan Larsson, Frederik Fabricius-Bjerre

items.title: A new approach for estimating the number of spikes in high-dimensional Gaussian models
items.abstract: In this paper, we study the estimation of the signal subspace dimension $k$ in a $p$-variate signal-plus-noise complex Gaussian model, when the noise covariance matrix is assumed to be diagonal or Toeplitz. We consider the high-dimensional asymptotic regime in which both the data dimension $p$ and the available sample size $n$ diverge to infinity at the same rate, while we also allow $k$ to diverge at a slower speed. In this context, the classical estimates of the literature, consistent in the high-dimensional regime, often rely on the a priori knowledge of an upper bound $k_*$ of $k$, which can be misspecified in practice. Our proposed approach relies on building estimates of the tracial moments of the noise covariance matrix using the $p-k_*$ smallest eigenvalues of the sample covariance matrix (SCM), which are in turn used to build a threshold above which the $k$ largest eigenvalues are isolated. The resulting estimate of $k$ is proved to be consistent in the high-dimensional regime, even for the misspecified situations where $k_* < k$. Numerical experiments in different challenging scenarios illustrate the improvement of the proposed approach over the aforementioned methods.
items.authors: Hugo Jeannin, Pascal Vallet, Florent Bouchard, Guillaume Ginolhac, Audrey Giremus

items.title: Interpolation and coherence in multiple testing
items.abstract: In the literature on multiple testing methods that control the familywise error rate, a fundamental concept is "coherence". A procedure is coherent if it is "logically consistent" (Hochberg and Tamhane, 1987) in the sense that if a hypothesis is rejected, then all hypotheses that imply it are also rejected. If a method is not coherent, then it can be made coherent without increasing the familywise error rate. Recently, the concept of coherence was generalized to a much broader class of multiple testing procedures, namely all methods that provide simultaneous confidence bounds for false discovery proportions. Such procedures were defined to be coherent if they cannot be further improved through a process called "interpolation". However, we show that such a coherent procedure can sometimes be further improved by exploiting remaining logical inconsistencies. This leads to what we call a "perfectly coherent" method. Thus, interpolation does not necessarily lead to perfect coherence. However, we provide conditions under which it does. Fortunately, many methods based on interpolation turn out to be perfectly coherent.
items.authors: Ninh Tran, Dennis Leung, Jesse Hemerik

items.title: Strategic Multi-Agent Resource Allocation via Statistical Contracts
items.abstract: We study a class of strategic hypothesis testing problems in which a principal aims to allocate resources among competing agents who possess data or data-generating mechanisms that may be relevant to the principal's goals. Each agent can pay a participation cost to opt into a statistical contract, in which case they generate data from a private distribution and receive an allocation based on a predetermined (and publicly known) mechanism. Each agent is either "null" or "non-null" and the principal's goal is to design the contract to limit the allocation to the former while maximizing transactions with the latter. Using e-values, we define a "continuous-closure," a set of allocations which prevents null agents from profiting in expectation and provides post-hoc risk control for general loss functions under arbitrary dependence. When the loss is the fraction of resources allocated to null agents, the region admits polynomial-time linear optimization. We also give explicit, interpretable closed-form approximations, and we analyze participation from a non-null agent's perspective, giving conditions under which entry into the contract is profitable. Finally, we extend the framework to support online arrival of the agents, in which case the principal has to make irrevocable on-the-fly decisions, and provide a method which gives time-uniform error-control in this setting.
items.authors: Ben Chugg, Michael I. Jordan, Aaditya Ramdas

items.title: Risk Measures for the Climate Transition Age: Why Symmetric Risk Budgets are unlikely to mitigate two-dimensionally asymmetric Climate Change risks
items.abstract: The most widely used investment risk measures - variance, standard deviation, and tracking error - treat upside deviations as equally undesirable as downside losses. In stable markets with assumed symmetric return distributions, this simplification is potentially harmless. In the climate transition age, it is not. Climate risk is two-dimensionally asymmetric, across assets and over time. Both dimensions are negatively skewed against investors. Hence, climate transition investment strategies deliberately deviate from benchmarks that reflect an insufficiently decarbonising global economy. When fiduciaries enforce tracking error budgets that penalise outperformance just as heavily as underperformance, they inadvertently constrain exactly the portfolio return opportunities that climate-aware investing seeks. We argue that replacing symmetric deviation-based risk measures with their downside-only counterparts - semi-variance, standard risk and trailing error - resolves this conflict without sacrificing any fiduciary discipline. The distinction is not merely semantic: as the gap between climate transition trajectories and market benchmarks widens over the coming decades, symmetric risk budgets will become binding constraints on transition strategies well before actual investment risk warrants it. We propose specific changes to mandate design that would allow institutional investors to pursue climate transition opportunities within genuinely risk-aware (rather than deviation-averse) frameworks.
items.authors: Lars Dijkstra, Andreas G. F. Hoepner, Fabiola I. Schneider, Agnieszka S{\l}omka-Go{\l}\k{e}biowska

items.title: Inference for Fr\'echet Mean Sets
items.abstract: We construct confidence sets for the entire Fr\'echet mean set by inverting studentized pairwise risk inequalities. Gaussian multiplier calibration localized around empirical near minimizers gives asymptotic coverage at least the nominal level, uniformly over distribution classes satisfying empirical-process conditions. The construction requires neither unique ness nor a manifold structure. We characterize the limiting binding directions and give conditions for exact asymptotic coverage. On the intrinsic circle, exactness holds for every fixed non-point-mass law and uniformly over a family in which two means merge at a quar tic minimum. With ideal multiplier quantiles, the construction reproduces the Euclidean Wald set under both nonsingular and singular covariance. Under regular local conditions, it is first-order equivalent to intrinsic Wald inference.
items.authors: Ryunosuke Miyazaki

items.title: Information-Enriched Selection of Stationary and Non-Stationary Autoregressions using the Adaptive Lasso
items.abstract: We propose a novel approach to elicit the weight of a potentially non-stationary regressor in the consistent and oracle-efficient estimation of autoregressive models using the adaptive Lasso. The enhanced weight builds on a statistic that exploits distinct orders in probability of the OLS estimator in time series regressions when the degree of integration differs. We provide theoretical results on the benefit of our approach for detecting stationarity when a tuning criterion selects the $\ell_1$ penalty parameter. Monte Carlo evidence shows that our proposal is superior to using OLS-based weights, as suggested by Kock [Econom. Theory, 32, 2016, 243-259]. We apply the modified estimator to model selection for German inflation rates after the introduction of the Euro. The results indicate that energy commodity price inflation and headline inflation are best described by stationary autoregressions.
items.authors: Thilo Reinschl\"ussel, Martin C. Arnold

items.title: Inference for Heterogeneous Graphical Models using Doubly High-Dimensional Linear-Mixed Models
items.abstract: Inferring the structure of population-level functional connectivity networks from multi-subject functional magnetic resonance imaging data is essential for understanding the connectivity patterns underlying cognitive and behavioral functions. Graphical models provide a formal statistical framework for inferring the graph structure. However, the multi-level nature of functional magnetic resonance imaging data---where each level corresponds, for instance, to a subject---compromises the inferential validity of most existing methods. In this paper, we develop a valid inference framework for high-dimensional graphical models that accounts for cross-level heterogeneity. We introduce a neighborhood-based method to learn the graph structure and reframe the problem as that of inferring fixed effect parameters in a doubly high-dimensional linear mixed model. We then propose a LASSO-based estimator and a de-biased LASSO-based inference framework for these fixed effect parameters. We evaluate the performance of the proposed framework using benchmark simulation studies and apply it to descriptively compare graph structures between the functional connectivity networks of two predefined groups of subjects from the Human Connectome Project.
items.authors: Kun Yue, Eardi Lila, Ali Shojaie

items.title: Direction Preferring Confidence Intervals
items.abstract: Confidence intervals (CIs) are fundamental in statistical analysis, providing interval estimates for unknown parameters. We introduce direction-preferring CIs that prioritize inference for parameters with a specific sign (e.g., positive sign). Unlike previous methods of constructing CIs, our intervals are based on the inversion of acceptance regions that differ for positive and negative parameters, to enhance the probability of determining the sign in the prespecified preferred direction while maintaining standard coverage. We apply our suggestion in the typical context that multiple parameters are considered, but only some of the constructed CIs are of interest, e.g., when CIs are reported only for the subset of parameters that are found to differ significantly from zero. This leads us to suggest direction-preferring CIs with false coverage rate (FCR) control, as well as conditional direction-preferring CIs that adjust for selection by conditioning on the selection event. We compare the two selection adjustment methods in theory and using numerical experiments. The procedures we develop are useful for inference on secondary outcomes in medical applications, a setting we highlight through two motivating examples.
items.authors: Tzviel Frostig, Orestis A. Panagiotou, Yoav Benjamini, Ruth Heller

items.title: Adaptive Unit Root Inference in Autoregressions using the Lasso Solution Path
items.abstract: We show that the activation knot of a potentially non-stationary regressor on the adaptive Lasso solution path in autoregressions can be leveraged for selection-free inference about a unit root. The resulting test has asymptotic power against local alternatives in $1/T$ neighbourhoods, unlike post-selection inference methods based on consistent model selection. Exploiting the information enrichment principle devised by Reinschl\"ussel and Arnold (arXiv:2402.16580 [stat.ME]) to improve the Lasso-based selection of ADF models, we propose a composite statistic and analyse its asymptotic distribution and local power function. Monte Carlo evidence shows that the combined test dominates the comparable post-selection inference methods of Tibshirani et al. [JASA, 2016, 514, 600-620] and may surpass the power of established unit root tests against local alternatives. We apply the new tests to groundwater level time series for Germany and find evidence rejecting stochastic trends to explain observed long-term declines in mean water levels.
items.authors: Martin C. Arnold, Thilo Reinschl\"ussel

items.title: Exploring Exchangeability within Permutation Inference: Implications for Statistics and Data Science Educators
items.abstract: Permutation tests are a powerful and flexible approach to inference via resampling. As computational methods become more ubiquitous in the statistics curriculum, use of permutation tests has become more tractable. At the heart of the permutation approach is the *exchangeability condition*, which determines the appropriate null sampling distribution. We explore the exchangeability condition in the context of permutation tests, including settings where the exchangeability condition is not tenable. Our examples include two-sample comparisons of means, clustered designs, multiple linear regression, and two-sample comparisons of correlation. The different exchangeability challenges in each example allow further exploration of the definition and importance of the exchangeability requirement for permutation testing. We believe that understanding the exchangeability condition and how it relates to the null hypothesis gives students the skills to work effectively with permutation tests in more complicated modeling settings and to further their understanding of statistical inference. We close with pedagogical recommendations for instructors who wish to incorporate permutation inference into their curriculum as a means to increase student understanding of resampling-based inference.
items.authors: Johanna Hardin, Lauren Quesada, Julie Ye, Nicholas J. Horton

items.title: Bootstrap Adaptive Lasso Solution Path Unit Root Tests
items.abstract: We propose sieve wild bootstrap analogues to the adaptive Lasso solution path unit root tests of Arnold and Reinschl\"ussel (2024) arXiv:2404.06205 to improve finite sample properties and extend their applicability to a generalised framework, allowing for non-stationary volatility. Numerical evidence shows the bootstrap to improve the tests' precision for error processes that promote spurious rejections of the unit root null, depending on the detrending procedure. The bootstrap mitigates finite-sample size distortions and restores asymptotically valid inference when the data features time-varying unconditional variance. We apply the bootstrap tests to real residential property prices of the top six Eurozone economies and find evidence of stationarity to be period-specific, supporting the conjecture that exuberance in the housing market characterises the development of Euro-era residential property prices in the recent past.
items.authors: Martin C. Arnold, Thilo Reinschl\"ussel

items.title: Simulations for estimation of random effects and overall effect in three-level meta-analysis of standardized mean differences using constant and inverse-variance weights
items.abstract: We consider a three-level meta-analysis of standardized mean differences. The standard method of estimation uses inverse-variance weights and REML/PL estimation of variance components for the random effects. We introduce new moment-based point and interval estimators for the two variance components and related estimators of the overall mean. Similar to traditional analysis of variance, our method is based on two conditional $Q$ statistics with effective-sample-size weights. We study, by simulation, bias and coverage of these new estimators. For comparison, we also study bias and coverage of the REML/PL-based approach as implemented in {\it rma.mv} in {\it metafor}. Our results demonstrate that the new methods are often considerably better and do not have convergence problems, which plague the standard analysis.
items.authors: Elena Kulinskaya, David C. Hoaglin

items.title: WMAP: An R Package for Causal Meta-Analysis by Integrating Multiple Observational Studies
items.abstract: Integrating multiple observational studies for meta-analysis has sparked much interest. The presented R package WMAP (Weighted Meta-Analysis with Pseudo-Populations) (Guha et al., 2026) addresses a critical gap in the implementation of integrative weighting approaches for multiple observational studies and causal inferences about various groups of subjects, such as disease subtypes. The package features three weighting approaches, each representing a special case of the unified weighting framework introduced by Guha and Li (2024), which includes an extension of inverse probability weights for data integration settings. It performs meta-analysis on user-inputted datasets as follows: (i) it first estimates the propensity scores for study-group combinations, calculates subject balancing weights, and determines the effective sample size (ESS) for a user-specified weighting method; and (ii) it then estimates various features of multiple counterfactual group outcomes, such as group medians and differences in group means for the mRNA expression of eight genes. Additionally, bootstrap variability estimates are provided. Among the implemented weighting methods, we highlight the FLEXible, Optimized, and Realistic (FLEXOR) method, which is specifically designed to maximize the ESS within the unified framework. The use of the software is illustrated through simulations and a multi-site breast cancer case study based on a simulated dataset modeled after real TCGA data from seven medical centers.
items.authors: Subharup Guha, Mengqi Xu, Chayce Reed, Kashish Priyam, Yi Li

items.title: Targeted Data Fusion for Region-Specific Survival Effects in the AMP HIV Prevention Trials
items.abstract: The Antibody Mediated Prevention (AMP) trials opened a new scientific frontier by showing that passively administered monoclonal broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) could prevent HIV-1 acquisition. The trials enrolled 4,611 participants across four epidemiologically distinct regions, with 174 HIV-1 diagnoses observed during follow-up. Regional heterogeneity in treatment efficacy, together with privacy and regulatory limits on central data pooling, calls for methods that borrow strength across regions without sharing individual-level data. To estimate region- and treatment-specific survival curves under distributional heterogeneity, we develop a federated learning approach that combines site-specific estimators via an L1-regularized criterion that downweights data sources not aligned with the target. We further extend the framework to a general class of causal contrasts, including the survival difference, survival ratio, and restricted mean survival time difference. In the AMP analysis, for example, the standard error of the day-148 survival difference decreased from 0.007 using the target-only estimator to 0.004 using the federated estimator. For women in South Africa, the region-specific analyses provided no strong evidence of an overall VRC01 benefit, consistent with the primary AMP findings. Overall, the proposed approach provides region-adaptive inference with improved precision without sharing individual-level data, while preserving estimation of region-specific treatment effects under cross-region heterogeneity.
items.authors: Yi Liu, Alexander W. Levis, Ke Zhu, Shu Yang, Peter B. Gilbert, Larry Han

items.title: Bayesian local clustering of functional data via semi-Markovian random partitions
items.abstract: We introduce a Bayesian framework for indirect local clustering of functional data, leveraging B-spline basis expansions and a novel dependent random partition model. By exploiting the local support properties of B-splines, our approach allows partially coincident functional behaviors, achieved when shared basis coefficients span sufficiently contiguous regions. This is accomplished through a cutting-edge dependent random partition model that enforces semi-Markovian dependence across a sequence of partitions. By matching the degree of the B-spline basis with the semi-Markovian dependence structure, the proposed model serves as a highly flexible prior, enabling efficient modeling of localized features in functional data. Furthermore, we extend the utility of the dependent random partition model beyond functional data, demonstrating its applicability to a broad class of problems where sequences of dependent partitions are central, and standard Markovian assumptions prove overly restrictive. Empirical illustrations, including analyses of simulated data and tide level measurements from the Venice Lagoon, showcase the effectiveness and versatility of the proposed methodology.
items.authors: Giovanni Toto, Antonio Canale

items.title: A longitudinal Bayesian framework for estimating causal dose-response relationships
items.abstract: Existing causal methods for time-varying exposure and time-varying confounding focus on estimating the average causal effect of a time-varying binary treatment on an end-of-study outcome, offering limited tools for characterizing marginal causal dose-response relationships under continuous exposures. We propose a scalable, nonparametric Bayesian framework for estimating marginal longitudinal causal dose-response functions with repeated outcome measurements. Our approach targets the average potential outcome at any fixed dose level and accommodates time-varying confounding through the generalized propensity score. The proposed approach embeds a Dirichlet process specification within a generalized estimating equations structure, capturing temporal correlation while making minimal assumptions about the functional form of the continuous exposure. We apply the proposed methods to monthly metro ridership and COVID-19 case data from major international cities, identifying causal relationships and the dose-response patterns between higher ridership and increased case counts.
items.authors: Yu Luo, Kuan Liu, Ramandeep Singh, Daniel J. Graham

items.title: Dependent Dirichlet processes via thinning
items.abstract: When analyzing data from multiple sources, it is often convenient to strike a careful balance between two goals: capturing the heterogeneity of the samples and sharing information across them. We introduce a novel framework to model a collection of samples using dependent Dirichlet processes constructed through a thinning mechanism. The proposed approach modifies the stick-breaking representation of the Dirichlet process by thinning, that is, setting equal to zero a random subset of the beta random variables used in the original construction. This results in a collection of dependent random distributions that exhibit both shared and unique atoms, with the shared ones assigned distinct weights in each distribution. The generality of the construction allows expressing a wide variety of dependence structures among the elements of the generated random vectors. Moreover, its simplicity facilitates the characterization of several theoretical properties and the derivation of efficient computational methods for posterior inference. A simulation study illustrates how a modeling approach based on the proposed process reduces uncertainty in group-specific inferences while preventing excessive borrowing of information when the data indicate it is unnecessary. This added flexibility improves the accuracy of posterior inference, outperforming related state-of-the-art models. An application to the Collaborative Perinatal Project data highlights the model's capability to estimate group-specific densities and uncover a meaningful partition of the observations, both within and across samples, providing valuable insights into the underlying data structure.
items.authors: Laura D'Angelo, Bernardo Nipoti, Andrea Ongaro

items.title: Assumption-Lean Differential Variance Inference for Heterogeneous Treatment Effect Detection
items.abstract: The conditional average treatment effect (CATE) is frequently estimated in clinical studies to refute a homogeneous treatment effect hypothesis. Under this regime, all patients making up the population experience identical benefit from a given treatment relative to a comparator. Uncovering heterogeneous treatment effects through inference about the CATE, however, requires that covariates truly modifying the treatment effect be reliably collected at baseline. CATE-based techniques will necessarily fail to detect violations when effect modifiers are omitted from the data due to, for example, resource constraints. Severe measurement error has a similar impact. Clinical decision makers can be misled as a result. To address these limitations, we prove that a practical homogeneous treatment effect hypothesis can be gauged through inference about contrasts of the potential outcomes' variances even when effect modifiers are missing from the data. We derive causal machine learning estimators of these contrasts and study their asymptotic properties. We establish that these estimators are doubly robust and asymptotically linear under mild conditions, permitting formal hypothesis testing about treatment effect heterogeneity. Numerical experiments demonstrate that these estimators' asymptotic guarantees are approximately achieved in finite-sample randomized and observational study data alike. These inference procedures are then used to detect heterogeneous treatment effects in the re-analysis of randomized controlled trials investigating targeted temperature management in cardiac arrest patients.
items.authors: Philippe A. Boileau, Hani Zaki, Gabriele Lileikyte, Niklas Nielsen, Patrick R. Lawler, Mireille E. Schnitzer

items.title: Detecting Impact of the Great Recession on Macroeconomic Indicators
items.abstract: We study structural changes in multivariate time series by estimating and comparing stationary graphs of macroeconomic time series before and after an economic crisis, such as the Great Recession. Building on a latent time series framework called Orthogonally-rotated Univariate Time-series (OUT), we propose a shared-parameter framework-the spOUT autoregressive model (spOUTAR)-that jointly models two related multivariate time series and enables coherent Bayesian estimation of their corresponding stationary precision matrices. This framework provides a principled mechanism for detecting and quantifying which conditional relationships among the variables changed or formed following the crisis. Specifically, we study the impact of the Great Recession (December 2007-June 2009) that substantially disrupted global and national economies, prompting long-lasting shifts in macroeconomic indicators and their interrelationships. While many studies document its economic consequences, less is known about how the underlying conditional dependency structure among economic variables changed as economies moved from pre-crisis stability through the shock and back to normalcy. Using the proposed approach to analyze U.S. and OECD macroeconomic data, we demonstrate that spOUTAR effectively captures recession-induced changes in stationary graphical structure, offering a flexible and interpretable tool for studying structural shifts in economic systems.
items.authors: Shuvrarghya Ghosh, Arkaprava Roy, Anindya Roy, Subhashis Ghosal

items.title: Fully Bayesian Spectral Clustering and Benchmarking with Uncertainty Quantification for Small Area Estimation
items.abstract: In this work, inspired by machine learning techniques, we propose a new Bayesian model for Small Area Estimation (SAE), the Fay-Herriot model with Spectral Clustering (FH-SC). Unlike traditional approaches, clustering in FH-SC is based on spectral clustering algorithms that utilize external covariates, rather than geographical or administrative criteria. A major advantage of the FH-SC model is its flexibility in integrating existing SAE approaches, with or without clustering random effects. To enable benchmarking, we leverage the theoretical framework of posterior projections for constrained Bayesian inference and derive closed form expressions for the new Rao-Blackwell (RB) estimators of the posterior mean under the FH-SC model. Additionally, we introduce a novel measure of uncertainty for the benchmarked estimator, the Conditional Posterior Mean Square Error (CPMSE), which is generalizable to other Bayesian SAE estimators. We conduct model-based and data-based simulation studies to evaluate the frequentist properties of the CPMSE. The proposed methodology is motivated by a real case study involving the estimation of the proportion of households with internet access in the municipalities of Colombia. Finally, we also illustrate the advantages of FH-SC over existing Bayesian and frequentist approaches through our case study.
items.authors: Jairo F\'uquene-Pati\~no

items.title: Coherent Information Deletion: Bayesian, Generalized Bayesian and Possibilistic Unlearning
items.abstract: Bayes' theorem admits an information processing interpretation due to Zellner (1988): under the Shannon information criterion, the posterior is the unique rule that processes prior and data information without information loss. We revisit these ideas from the perspective of information deletion. Given a posterior based on a complete dataset, what distribution should replace it when a subset of the data is removed? For ordinary Bayesian inference, we show that the corresponding information deletion objective is uniquely minimized by the leave-data-out posterior. We then extend the framework beyond likelihood-based inference from Bayes to the generalized Bayesian updating of Bissiri et al.(2016} based on loss functions. Requiring deletion to be coherent under sequential removal of loss contributions yields a deletion rule that exactly recovers the generalized posterior based only on the retained information. We further develop an axiomatic theory, beyond probabilistic inference, for possibilistic deletion and show that the same information-deletion perspective leads to a principled rule for exact possibilistic unlearning. Finally, restricting these exact deletion principles to tractable families leads naturally to variational Bayesian, generalized Bayesian, and maxitive possibilistic unlearning.
items.authors: Hans Montcho, H{\aa}vard Rue, Maurizio Filippone
items.title_zh: 一致性信息删除：贝叶斯、广义贝叶斯与可能性去学习
items.summary_zh: 本文基于Zellner（1988）的观点，重新审视了贝叶斯定理的信息处理解释，探讨在信息删除的背景下，如何在移除数据子集后替换完整数据集的后验分布。我们证明，对于普通贝叶斯推断，相应的信息删除目标由留数据后的后验唯一最小化。进一步扩展至基于损失函数的Bissiri等人（2016）的广义贝叶斯更新，要求在顺序移除损失贡献时保持一致性，得出仅基于保留信息的广义后验的删除规则。此外，我们发展了超越概率推断的公理化理论，针对可能性删除，展示相同的信息删除视角如何导出精确的可能性去学习规则。最后，将这些精确删除原则限制在可处理的家族中，自然引出变分贝叶斯、广义贝叶斯和最大化可能性去学习。

items.title: Prior Smoothing for Multivariate Disease Mapping Models
items.abstract: To date, we have seen the emergence of a large literature on multivariate disease mapping. That is, incidence of (or mortality from) multiple diseases is recorded at the scale of areal units where incidence (mortality) across the diseases is expected to manifest dependence. The modeling involves a hierarchical structure: a Poisson model for disease counts (conditioning on the rates) at the first stage, and a specification of a function of the rates using spatial random effects at the second stage. These random effects are specified as a prior and introduce spatial smoothing to the rate (or risk) estimates. What we see in the literature is the amount of smoothing induced under a given prior across areal units compared with the observed/empirical risks. Our contribution here extends previous research on smoothing in univariate areal data models. Specifically, for three different choices of multivariate prior, we investigate both within prior smoothing according to hyperparameters and across prior smoothing. Its benefit to the user is to illuminate the expected nature of departure from perfect fit associated with these priors, providing measures of their smoothing behavior not captured by conventional measures of predictive performance. We propose both theoretical and empirical metrics for our investigation and illustrate with both simulated and real data.
items.authors: Garazi Retegui, Mar\'ia Dolores Ugarte, Jaione Etxeberria, Alan E. Gelfand

items.title: Design-based theory for covariate adjustment in generalized pairwise comparisons
items.abstract: Generalized pairwise comparisons summarize treatment effects in randomized experiments with ordinal, multivariate, or prioritized outcomes. We study optimal covariate adjustment under complete randomization, with potential outcomes and covariates fixed and treatment assignment as the sole source of randomness. We derive the exact randomization variance of the unadjusted estimator and characterize linear calibration adjustments using the between-arm difference in covariate means. The asymptotic variance is a strictly convex quadratic in the adjustment coefficient, yielding a closed-form optimum. The resulting estimator is asymptotically no less efficient than the unadjusted estimator, with an explicit precision gain that clarifies which covariates improve precision. However, natural pair-level and single-arm least squares adjustments generally use weights that differ from the allocation-dependent optimum and can substantially reduce efficiency. We also propose a within-arm variance estimator for asymptotically conservative inference, whose conservatism arises from unidentifiable joint variation in a unit's two potential scores, and show that residualizing each arm on its own projection coefficient saves the discrepancy that governs the efficiency loss of conventional adjustments. In the special case where the comparison function is the outcome difference, our proposed covariate-adjusted estimator is first-order equivalent to the fully interacted regression adjustment of Lin (Ann. Appl. Stat., 2013, 7, 295-318).
items.authors: Xinyuan Chen, Fan Li

items.title: Transportable inference using target population summary statistics under covariate shift
items.abstract: Transporting findings from a study population to a target population is central to evidence-based decision-making in real-world settings. Most existing methods require individual-level data from both populations to account for covariate shift. However, privacy regulations and data-sharing constraints often preclude access to such data from the target population, leaving only covariate summaries available for analysis. In this paper, we develop transportability methods that enable valid inference using source individual-level data and target covariate summaries. First, we apply entropy balancing to transportability, enabling source individual-level data to be adjusted to match the target covariate moments. We establish asymptotic normality for the entropy balancing estimator and propose a variance estimator to account for uncertainty in covariate summaries. Second, we develop a new transportability method that allows more flexible modeling of covariate shift, thereby accounting for covariate shift and uncertainty in covariate summaries simultaneously. Asymptotic normality for the proposed estimator is established and its asymptotic variance is consistently estimated. The proposed method offers greater flexibility in accounting for covariate shift and thus permits consistent estimation and valid inference when the validity of entropy balancing is not guaranteed. The proposed methods are evaluated by simulations and illustrated with an analysis of Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results breast cancer data.
items.authors: Ying Sheng, Yifei Sun, Chiung-Yu Huang

items.title: Claims, Designs, and Guarantees: A Critical Narrative Review of Statistical Inference Reform and Practice, 2016--2026
items.abstract: Statistics helps scientists decide what their data show, but its most familiar tool, the $p$-value, is widely misunderstood. Between 2016 and 2026, professional bodies issued new guidance, and researchers developed or popularised alternatives and complements: compatibility intervals, equivalence tests, Bayes factors, and e-values that remain valid when data are checked repeatedly. Reporting rules for trials and reviews were also rewritten. Yet practice has changed little: in the biomedical literature, about 96\% of papers that report $p$-values still include at least one below 0.05. This review argues that much of the confusion comes from treating these numbers as interchangeable. Each inferential procedure carries an intended interpretation and, where applicable, a formal guarantee, such as a 5\% false-alarm rate, that holds only if the study was run and analysed in a particular way. We call this the Claim--Design--Guarantee framework: a result licenses a claim only when the claim, the design (assignment, sampling, monitoring, selection, and analysis), and the guarantee of the method are aligned. We trace the main developments of the decade, explain each tool in plain terms with formal details in boxes, and show with reproducible examples when the choice of tool changes the conclusion. For example, in a simulated two-group study with 100 interim looks, repeatedly applying an unadjusted $p<0.05$ rule produced false positives in 37.6\% of studies, whereas the particular anytime-valid e-value procedure we used produced 2.2\%, below its theoretical 5\% upper bound. We end with a decision tree, a method-selection table, and a step-by-step workflow linked to current reporting guidelines.
items.authors: Aswini Kumar Patra, Shashi Bhushan Jha

items.title: Kernel-based independence and mean independence tests for weakly dependent data
items.abstract: We provide a unified framework for independence and mean independence tests based on the Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion, extending some previous results in the literature to hold in general topological spaces. We also present a complete theoretical analysis of the test statistic asymptotic behavior when the observed sample corresponds to a partial sample path of some stationary and ergodic stochastic process under near epoch dependence assumptions. In particular, we explore the test statistic consistency and limit distribution under both fixed and local hypothesis. The finite sample performance of the test(s) is illustrated with a succinct simulation study involving functional data.
items.authors: Daniel Diz-Castro, Manuel Febrero-Bande, Wenceslao Gonz\'alez-Manteiga

items.title: Stabilised weighted data subsampling for accelerated Bayesian inference in models with recursive likelihoods
items.abstract: Bayesian inference for models with recursively defined likelihoods is computationally demanding, limiting scalability to large datasets. We propose a stabilised weighted subsampling methodology for accelerated Bayesian inference based on an unbiased estimator of the log-likelihood. By assigning higher sampling probabilities to early observations, the method reduces the effective depth of recursive likelihood evaluations and hence computational cost. This creates a challenging variance-cost trade-off: sampling probabilities that decay too slowly yield limited computational savings, while overly aggressive decay can substantially inflate estimator variance. We develop a stabilisation framework, supported by theory, that controls this trade-off and leads to a practical, theory-informed tuning strategy. We also derive an unbiased subsampling estimator of the log-likelihood gradient, enabling gradient-based Bayesian inference. The methodology can be embedded within a range of Bayesian computational algorithms. We illustrate its use in variational Bayes and subsampling Markov chain Monte Carlo for conditional volatility models, including leverage effects. Empirical results show substantial computational speed-ups relative to full-data methods while maintaining inferential accuracy. We also compare with recent stochastic gradient MCMC and divide-and-conquer MCMC methods for temporally dependent data, observing favourable empirical performance.
items.authors: Matias Quiroz, Aishwarya Bhaskaran, Zixuan Wang, Thomas Goodwin

items.title: Estimating marginal association between paired outcomes in clustered data with an application to analyzing caries and periodontal disease data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey
items.abstract: The within-cluster subgroup composition of units can inform on the marginal distribution of those units outcomes, denoted informative subgroup size (ISS). Moreover, within-cluster subgroup composition of paired outcomes can allow one outcome to inform upon the marginal distribution of the other. If this type of ISS ignored, it can bias marginal association estimates by allowing subgroup composition to influence how clusters contribute to the analysis. We develop two weighting approaches for estimating marginal association between paired outcomes in this setting. The weights are derived using within-cluster resampling arguments and extend conventional cluster weighting to paired response subgroups. We adapt an existing test of marginal dependence to assess ISS by examining this subgroup structure in both directions. In simulated data exhibiting this bidirectional ISS, pair-based weighting reduced bias when association was primarily carried through the paired observations. These weights also allow scientifically or clinically meaningful dichotomizations to enter directly into the weighting scheme, with the choice of subgroup definition further improving estimation in several simulated settings. Application to NHANES oral-health data showed strong evidence of ISS for filled-surface outcomes across subgroups defined by clinical attachment loss and pocket depth, with the corresponding periodontal--caries associations generally small and positive. These methods provide a practical approach for estimating marginal association when paired subgroup composition is informative.
items.authors: Owen Visser, Steven Levy, Bruce Dye, Shaoping Zhang, Victor Agboli, Somnath Datta

items.title: A stable method for direct estimation of single-index terms in GAMs with an application to bike-sharing demand
items.abstract: Single-index terms have been increasingly applied in generalized additive models (GAMs) across diverse areas due to their versatility in integrating functional flexibility with parametric dimension reduction while maintaining interpretability. However, the estimation presents severe computational challenges. This paper introduces a stable method based on Fisher scoring that dynamically updates the boundaries of the single-index covariates within a unified iterative framework using P-splines. Simulation studies with moderate sample sizes under non-Gaussian distributions confirm the empirical consistency of the estimation across multiple scenarios. Notably, the proposed method remains stable where state-of-the-art competitive methods fail to recover true single-index coefficients and their associated nonlinear functions, and is 80.13 times faster than the usual two-step method in the most computationally intensive scenario. The modeling advantage is illustrated through an application to Capital Bike Sharing data, where we deal with a single-index interaction effect for each year, with distinct single-index coefficients, a complex structure that makes competitive methods inapplicable. The proposed method is implemented in R, with all functions available at https://github.com/silva-danilo/sipgam for reproducibility and transparency in comparisons.
items.authors: Danilo V. Silva, Gilberto A. Paula

items.title: Estimation and Inference for Win Measures with Multiple Ordinal Endpoints Subject to Missingness
items.abstract: Win measures, including the win ratio, win odds, net benefit, and desirability of outcome ranking, are increasingly used in randomized clinical trials with multiple hierarchical ordinal endpoints. In practice, however, one or more component endpoints may have missing data. The standard pairwise-comparison approach, which treats pairs with missing outcomes as ties, can produce biased estimates, even if the data are missing completely at random. Although inverse probability of censoring weighting methods have been developed for censored survival endpoints, corresponding methods for addressing missing hierarchical ordinal endpoints are not yet available. To address this gap, we develop inverse probability weighted (IPW) and augmented IPW (AIPW) estimators for win measures with hierarchical ordinal endpoints subject to missing data, allowing missingness to depend on treatment assignment and baseline covariates. The IPW estimator corrects bias by reweighting complete observed outcomes using joint non-missingness probabilities involved in estimating the joint cell probabilities that define the win measures. The AIPW estimator additionally incorporates outcome modeling, potentially improving estimation precision and achieving double robustness. For inference, we derive closed-form variance estimators for both methods based on influence functions. Simulation studies show that the standard approach can be substantially biased, whereas the proposed IPW and AIPW estimators exhibit small bias and near-nominal coverage under their respective identifying and model conditions. Applications to the SCOUT-CAP and ACTT-1 trials illustrate the practical utility of the proposed methods. An R package WinMO is provided for implementation.
items.authors: Yi Liu, Huiman Barnhart, Sean O'Brien, Yuliya Lokhnygina, Roland A. Matsouaka

items.title: A Non-Stationary Spatio-Temporal Covariance Model with Dynamic Advection Effects for Rainfall Data
items.abstract: We propose a non-stationary model constructed using a mixture of spatio-temporal covariance models with advection effects; namely, models that have larger covariance values along an orientation vector in the spatio-temporal index set, that simulate wind direction and cloud movement. We show that a mixture of such models can allow for wind direction change in data during (estimated) time intervals, unlike traditional models that use rigid advection effects. We construct a MCMC procedure for Bayesian estimation, and illustrate the method with the analysis of a severe rainfall event from the southeastern region of Brazil.
items.authors: Pedro Nasevicius Ramos, Guilherme Ludwig

items.title: Functional Principal Component Analysis for Manifold-Indexed Data
items.abstract: Functional principal component analysis has traditionally focused on processes indexed by Euclidean domains, although functional observations increasingly arise on curved domains. We develop FPCA for real-valued processes observed with noise at discrete locations on a general Riemannian manifold. We estimate the mean and covariance functions using intrinsic kernel smoothing based on geodesic distance and a normal-coordinate volume correction, with a general weighting scheme accommodating unequal numbers of observations across subjects. We establish $L^2$ and uniform convergence rates for these estimators and derive corresponding error bounds for the estimated eigenvalues and eigenfunctions. These results quantify how manifold dimension, sampling frequency and weighting affect estimation accuracy and characterize the phase transition between sparse and dense sampling regimes. Simulation studies on the circle and sphere, together with real-data applications, illustrate the finite-sample performance of the proposed methodology.
items.authors: Chang Jun Im, Jeong Min Jeon

items.title: Mixtures of spatial factor analyzers for tensor-variate data
items.abstract: A mixture of spatial factor analyzers (MSFA) is introduced to address the challenges of clustering high-dimensional spatial data. The proposed framework utilizes the given coordinate system to implement a flexible, spline-based spatial decay covariance structure. In this approach, the number of covariance parameters increases linearly with the number of spatial locations, rather than increasing quadratically. To model non-spatial dependence, matrix variate factor analyzers are employed for further dimensionality reduction. Parameter estimation is conducted via a variant of the expectation-maximization algorithm combined with a generalized least squares estimator. The proposed models are explored in the context of tensor-variate data analysis, where simulation studies and three applications---Raman spectroscopy, SpecTex hyperspectral textures, and the Salinas hyperspectral scene---illustrate their ability to recover and distinguish spatial dependence patterns. The R implementation is available on CRAN: https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=SpatMix.
items.authors: Hanzhang Lu, Keiran Malott, Kirsty Milligan, Sanjeena Subedi, Edana Cassol, Vinita Chauhan, Connor McNairn, Prarthana Pasricha, Sangeeta Murugkar, Rowan M. Thomson, Andrew Jirasek, Jeffrey L. Andrews

items.title: The Debiased Score Test: Hunt-and-test for Semiparametric Hypotheses
items.abstract: The parametric score test assesses a hypothesis through derivatives of the log-likelihood, whose expectation vanishes under the null. When the parameter of interest is a regression function identified as a risk minimiser, we extend this idea to test whether it belongs to a given linear function class. This yields goodness-of-fit tests for common semiparametric regression models, including generalised additive and partially linear models. Suitably formulated, the framework also detects effect modifiers in observational studies. We propose a hunt-and-test strategy that splits the data into two: on one part, after fitting the null model, machine learning is used to identify a promising direction in the empirical scores; on the other, we test whether the score vanishes in that direction. To account for error in estimating the null model, we apply a debiasing correction based on a weighted least squares projection. We establish Type I error control under relatively mild conditions and show the test has power whenever the hunted direction is correlated with the true score. Simulations and real-data examples demonstrate favourable performance, including identifying effect modifiers in an HIV clinical trial and assessing an additive model for insurance claims. The methodology is implemented in the R package dScoreTest.
items.authors: Aditya Dhawan, F. Richard Guo, Rajen D. Shah

items.title: Conditional validity of prediction-powered inference for spatially dependent finite populations
items.abstract: Prediction-powered inference (PPI) combines full-frame predictions with a small labelled sample to estimate finite-population regression coefficients. We establish conditions for the conditional validity of existing calibrated residual-regression PPI estimators under nonuniform label acquisition and spatially dependent prediction errors. Approximate calibration can leave a population-specific displacement: the projection of prediction errors onto coefficient-specific calibration defects. We characterize its role in conditional inference through the noncentrality of a fixed-candidate Wald region. The relevant target-weight function is the coefficient loading divided by acquisition intensity. When mean-approximation error does not dominate, directional covariance control yields a wider sufficient recovery regime than a total residual-energy bound. A bounded spectral-basis theorem gives conditional coverage under directional covariance, tail and nondegeneracy conditions, with Gaussian and bounded non-Gaussian spatial examples. The analysis accounts for estimation of the one-step augmentation and permits same-label selection from a fixed finite library with a common first-order influence vector. A periodic Fourier construction attains the stochastic directional-gap order within a restricted dictionary class. Constructed and real-record-set experiments illustrate why mean calibration need not protect a slope. The results concern descriptive census projection coefficients under the stated sampling and field conditions.
items.authors: Shinichiro Shirota

items.title: Model-assisted estimation with a training subsample: a two-phase sampling approach with design-based variance estimation
items.abstract: When a flexible prediction model is fitted on a training subsample drawn from a probability sample, the model-assisted estimator actually reported arises from one realized partition, yet existing theory quantifies uncertainty only for partition-averaged, cross-fitted, or symmetrized versions of it. We represent the training subsample as a second phase of sampling and derive, exactly and for any algorithm, a two-term variance decomposition and the variance family linking the single-partition estimator to its Rao-Blackwellized average, whose design bias it shares. For cell-mean rules under equal-probability designs the estimator is, exactly, a convex combination of a poststratified plug-in at the training-sample size and the exactly unbiased single-split estimator of Sanguiao Sande and Zhang, which locates its bias precisely. For tree-type predictors the second-phase variance is computable in closed form when the cell structure is fixed or $s$-measurable, and in that regime, for cell counts $H=o(n)$, its share of total variance grows with the number of cells -- a design-based mechanism distinct from residual shrinkage and consistent with the variance underestimation documented for flexible learners. We propose an analytic and a replication variance estimator, neither altering the point estimate, and evaluate them by simulation under simple random and stratified designs, in the adaptive regime and in an $s$-measurable configuration in which the theory is exact: in the populations studied, budgeting the second phase recovers much of the coverage lost by ignoring it, and the residual shortfall is attributable to the bias of the point estimator rather than to its variance.
items.authors: Mar\'ia Eugenia Ria\~no

items.title: Dangers of Bayesian analyses and how to address them
items.abstract: In light of the US FDA announcement supporting the use of Bayesian methods in clinical trials, we present a nontechnical review of problems with Bayesian analyses and methods to address them. Our focus is on the well-known sensitivities of Bayesian results to biases embedded in their prior distributions. This vulnerability calls for special safety features, including detailed justification of informative priors based on empirical-research literature rather than on singular expert opinions. Crucially, the information contributed by priors should be realistic in light of actual background data rather than merely judged so by available experts. We illustrate our recommendations with using a textbook clinical-trial example which covered these points. We then use the example describe basic diagnostic procedures and safety recommendations for Bayesian analyses and their presentation. These include reference analyses which exclude informative priors, and justification for informative priors based on empirical-research literature rather than on philosophical arguments. We also critique some common priors that violate our realism requirements. One strategy to aid judgments about priors is to translate them into data to be added to the study data. The source of these prior data should be examined with the same critical attitude as the source of study data. We illustrate some simple summary methods for comparing prior and data information, including prior predictions of data, variance ratios, and their translation to effective sample sizes (ESS). Finally, we argue that Bayesian analyses should be treated as extensions or supplements to conventional analyses, rather than replace them, for that treatment puts prior construction and justification at the fore of the transition from frequentist to Bayesian analyses in teaching and practice.
items.authors: Sander Greenland, Jason Oke

items.title: Federated multiple testing with quantized p-values under family-wise error control
items.abstract: Several institutions test one family of hypotheses under family-wise error control but cannot pool their data, so each site releases only a quantized report of its p-value for each hypothesis, such as whether the p-value is significant. The report's resolution is the number of values it can take. We quantify the power lost to such reports relative to the most powerful centralized procedure given all p-values (the oracle), with reports and combining rule chosen optimally. A report from which the p-value can be recovered loses no power, so the loss is due to compression, not decentralization. Under the stated regularity and power-objective conditions, every finite resolution loses power, and the optimal loss decays as the inverse square of the resolution: equal-width intervals attain this order, and no partition into as many cells improves it. In two-site Beta examples, optimized one-bit reports are nearly lossless for a single hypothesis but lose several times as much power for two. At level 0.05 with two Beta(1,2) hypotheses, optimally combined three-bit equal-width reports retain 99.2% of oracle power. We give the power-optimal combining rule for given reports, and a rule using only their exactly known null distribution, valid under arbitrary dependence across hypotheses.
items.authors: Prasanjit Dubey, Xiaoming Huo

items.title: Identification problem and quasi-maximum likelihood estimation for matrix-variate CP-factor models
items.abstract: Matrix-valued time series, arising in diverse fields such as economics, neuroscience, and recommender systems, have become increasingly prominent in modern data analysis. Among various modeling frameworks, the matrix-variate CP-factor model represents an important and widely applicable class for capturing low-rank structures in matrix time series. In this paper, we provide a unified treatment for the identification problem of CP factor models using both analytic and algebraic tools. In particular, we characterize the parameter space as the union of two subspaces, one identifiable and the other non-identifiable. We show that existing estimation methods only apply to an open proper subset of the identifiable subspace. In contrast, we propose a quasi-maximum likelihood estimation (QMLE) procedure for CP factor models, which allows consistent estimation on the whole identifiable subspace. Moreover, we show that the estimated loading matrices by QMLE achieve a faster convergence rate compared to existing approaches. A simulation study and a real application are conducted to demonstrate the finite-sample performance of the proposed method.
items.authors: Hanzi Ye, Chun Yip Yau

items.title: Streaming PCA: averaging from a geometric perspective
items.abstract: We study principal component analysis (PCA) under memory constraints, a setting that is increasingly important in large-scale data analysis. Our focus is on Oja's algorithm, which is a one-pass, memory-efficient algorithm requiring only $O(p)$ storage in the rank-one case and $O(pk)$ storage for $k$- PCA. The main goal is to develop a procedure based on Oja's algorithm that is optimal without prior knowledge of the eigengap, which is otherwise needed to tune the learning rates effectively. We do this by first introducing a geometric perspective on the convergence of $k$-PCA: by embedding the Oja iterates into the exterior space, we establish an exact equivalence between $k$-PCA in the ambient space and $1$-PCA in the exterior space. This geometric viewpoint enables us to establish several convergence guarantees, including one based only on a single learning-rate schedule. Building on this geometric perspective, we develop an averaging theory for $k$-PCA and show that the resulting averaged estimator is adaptive: it achieves the nearly optimal convergence rate without prior knowledge of the eigengap. As an application, we construct memory-efficient estimators for elliptical component analysis (ECA) \cite{han2014scale,han2018eca}. Simulation studies and real data analysis are conducted to demonstrate the benefits of our proposed algorithms.
items.authors: Tuan Pham, Alessandro Rinaldo, Purnamrita Sarkar

items.title: GRACE: A General, Exact Changepoint Calculus
items.abstract: We introduce GRACE (the General Regime-Aware Changepoint Estimator), a general, globally exact multiple-changepoint detection and estimation framework in which arbitrary numbers of model parameters may change at or persist across estimated changepoint locations, and all permissible changepoint types and patterns of parameter sharing compete within a single $\ell_0$-penalized optimization. The analyst specifies which types of changepoints are permitted and which parameters each type must preserve, without specifying which changes actually occur, where they occur, or in what order. GRACE jointly estimates the number and locations of changepoints, the type of change at each location, the model fitted between changepoints, and all continuous parameters. As a direct consequence, GRACE can estimate models in which the slope persists across a mean shift. The generality of the framework is achieved through an exact dynamic-programming recursion that retains the accumulated fitting cost conditional on whichever parameters a subsequent change may preserve, tracking multiple parameters jointly when necessary. We establish the global exactness of the recursion and develop functional, penalty-based, and objective-bound pruning rules that eliminate candidates without sacrificing optimality. Ordinary optimal partitioning, FPOP, and CPOP are recovered as special cases, while piecewise-polynomial and seasonal models illustrate the broader range of permissible segment structures and transitions. The resulting framework supports heterogeneous changepoint types, parameter sharing across segments, and substantial parallel computation within a unified approach to exact changepoint estimation.
items.authors: Michael Grantham

items.title: Randomization inference on cell effects under absorbing treatment onset
items.abstract: In multiple-baseline experiments, staggered adoption designs, and stepped-wedge trials, every unit switches once from baseline to treatment at a randomized onset time and remains treated afterward. The treatment onsets in these designs are absorbing. Since such experiments often involve few heterogeneous units, randomization tests of the sharp null of no effect on any unit-period cell are common. Rejecting this null, however, implies that some effect exists somewhere, not that it is large, positive for most unit-periods, or persistent. To improve on this limitation, we study what can be established via randomization tests for bounded and quantile nulls on cell effects in absorbing onset designs. Under the assumption that a cell's potential outcome depends on its current treatment status and not on when treatment began, we establish finite-sample validity for both tests. We then develop the power theory for the bounded-null tests with a fixed number of units $N$ and a growing series length $T$ admitting $K_T$ onsets. The $p$-value against a fixed alternative decays as $K_T^{-N}$ up to a factor polylogarithmic in $T$, with lower bounds of the same order, so the onset window, not the series length, determines the power. Theory-implied guidelines for experiment planning are also provided.
items.authors: Xinyuan Chen

items.title: Sequential resetting procedures and false discovery rate
items.abstract: Data arrive sequentially, each associated with a null hypothesis. We develop testing procedures to locate intervals in which some null hypotheses fail, with false discovery rate (FDR) control. The new procedures are called sequential resetting procedures, and they are based on e-values and test supermartingales. We also develop a refined version of the procedures by dropping less informative data points before the block minimum of the test supermartingale in each rejection block. These procedures have explicit FDR bounds under two settings: a classic setting of independence and the more general setting of possible dependence across null data and non-null data. These FDR bounds are independent of the testing horizon, and the general one has anytime validity, but it has an extra logarithm factor compared with the standard FDR level. We present simulation studies and data experiments with applications of sequential resetting procedures to LLM watermark detection and financial backtesting.
items.authors: Qiuqi Wang, Ruodu Wang, Zhenyuan Zhang

items.title: Anchored multiple testing: a transparent use of e-closure to improve FDR procedures
items.abstract: The recent e-closure method can recover every procedure that controls FDR (and other expectation losses). But the recovered e-collection is ``self-referential'' and gives no insight on how to improve the procedure (if improvable), and some recent improvements have been somewhat opaque. We introduce an elementary new technique called anchoring that exploits looseness in existing FDR proofs to enlarge a baseline multiple-testing procedure's self-referential local e-value. The resulting e-closure thus transparently retains every baseline discovery (and usually adding more) and controlling the false discovery rate under the same conditions as the baseline. To show that this principle is broadly applicable, we use it to improve a large suite of multiple testing procedures: (i) Anchored-BH dominates the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure under PRDS while being incomparable to Goeman's recent closed-BH, (ii) Anchored-BY dominates the Benjamini-Yekutieli (BY) procedure under arbitrary dependence while being incomparable to closed-BY, (iii) For two-sided Gaussian p-values (under appropriate covariance conditions), Anchored-2BH dominates running BH twice at half the level on two one-sided p-values, (iv) Anchored-dBH dominates dependence-adjusted BH, (v) Anchored e-BH dominates e-BH and is incomparable to closed e-BH, (vi) Anchored SeqStep+ improves the original (including selective and adpative variants) while preserving ordered rejection structures. All of these are accomplished in sorting or quadratic time. The appendix shows how to dominate Shifted-BH (for two-sided arbitrarily correlated Gaussians) and NDBH (for negatively dependent p-values), IndBH (for graph-dependent p-values), some online FDR procedures and the support line procedure for boundary FDR control.
items.authors: Aaditya Ramdas

items.title: Sequential Conformal Calibration under Recursive Selection
items.abstract: Conformal prediction provides finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantees that can support decision-making in specific settings. In multistage problems, earlier decisions determine the populations relevant to later calibration. When later scores are refit using earlier calibration results, reusing those cases for ranking need not preserve exchangeability with a surviving test case. We study sequential conformal calibration with a fresh fold at each stage: conditional on earlier folds, the selected fold scores and the surviving test score are exchangeable. This yields finite-sample coverage guarantees for every prefix of the decision sequence. For atomless survivor score distributions, we derive a universal Binomial-thinned Beta chain for the realized coverage process. Its law depends only on fold sizes and target levels, even under predictable refitting, and yields exact coverage slack, abstention probabilities, and calibration-conditional guarantees. We further characterize the tradeoff between freshness and data reuse. For fixed scores, strict-survivor reuse is exactly valid. For adaptive scores refit using past calibration data, reusing survivors can incur worst-case rank loss, while blocked designs provide an intermediate option between full reuse and stagewise fresh folds. As a case study, we apply the framework to serial multi-echelon inventory problem and propose a sequential conditional-quantile formulation. Each stock level is learned as a context-dependent quantile of cumulative demand among scenarios satisfying earlier no-backlog constraints. We connect these targets to common-shift stationarity and derive decision-level implications for the resulting calibrated policies. In a three-echelon simulation, fresh-fold refitting achieves 81.98% final-prefix coverage against an 81.82% target while reducing mean cost by 5.5% relative to the Bonferroni baseline.
items.authors: Yuning Yang, Zexuan Liu, Tianci Wang, Danlin Li

items.title: SLICE: Sequential Likelihood-Free Inference via Conformal E-Values
items.abstract: Many scientific models can be simulated but have intractable likelihoods, making frequentist uncertainty quantification difficult. We construct exact anytime-valid confidence sequences for the parameters of such models. At each observation, fresh simulations from each candidate null conformalize a positive predictable score into a conditional e-value; their product is a test martingale, which we invert over the parameter. Validity holds for any such score, whatever its accuracy. We show that the oracle likelihood-ratio score maximizes expected log growth, which motivates approximating it with an amortized neural ratio estimator. On synthetic benchmarks, an audit of model routing in an LLM API, and microlensing data, the resulting confidence sequences stay valid under continuous monitoring, where fixed-sample methods do not, and neural scores remain competitive with exact likelihood ratios and application-specific scores.
items.authors: Stefano Cortinovis, Laura Battaglia, Fran\c{c}ois Caron

items.title: Testing for an Explosive Bubble using High-Frequency Volatility
items.abstract: Based on a continuous-time stochastic volatility model with a linear drift, we develop a test for explosive behavior in financial asset prices at a low frequency when prices are sampled at a higher frequency. The test exploits the volatility information in the high-frequency data. The method consists of devolatizing log-asset price increments with realized volatility measures and performing a supremum-type recursive Dickey-Fuller test on the devolatized sample. The proposed test has a nuisance-parameter-free asymptotic distribution and is easy to implement. We study the size and power properties of the test in Monte Carlo simulations. A real-time date-stamping strategy based on the devolatized sample is proposed for the origination and conclusion dates of the explosive regime. Conditions under which the real-time date-stamping strategy is consistent are established. The test and the date-stamping strategy are applied to study explosive behavior in cryptocurrency and stock markets.
items.authors: H. Peter Boswijk, Jun Yu, Yang Zu

items.title: Stein's unbiased risk estimate and Hyv\"arinen's score matching
items.abstract: Given a collection of observed signals corrupted with Gaussian noise, how can we learn to optimally denoise them? This fundamental problem arises in both empirical Bayes and generative modeling. In empirical Bayes, the predominant approach is via nonparametric maximum likelihood estimation (NPMLE), while in generative modeling, score matching (SM) methods have proven very successful. In our setting, Hyv\"arinen's implicit SM is equivalent to another classical idea from statistics---Stein's Unbiased Risk Estimate (SURE). Revisiting SURE minimization, we establish, for the first time, that SURE achieves nearly parametric rates of convergence of the regret in the classical empirical Bayes setting with homoscedastic noise. We also prove that SURE-training can achieve fast rates of convergence to the oracle denoiser in a commonly studied misspecified model. We show how to practically implement our method in settings involving heteroscedasticity and side-information, such as in an application to the estimation of economic mobility in the Opportunity Atlas. Our empirical results demonstrate the superior performance of SURE-training over NPMLE under misspecification. Collectively, our findings advance SURE/SM as a strong alternative to the NPMLE for empirical Bayes problems in both theory and practice.
items.authors: Sulagna Ghosh, Nikolaos Ignatiadis, Frederic Koehler, Amber Lee

items.title: An Infinite BART model
items.abstract: Bayesian additive regression trees (BART) is a popular Bayesian ensemble model used in regression and classification analysis. Under this modeling framework, the regression function is approximated by an ensemble of decision trees, interpreted as weak learners. In this work, we propose a generalization of the BART model that has two main features: first, it automatically selects the number of decision trees using the given data; second, the model allows clusters of observations to have different regression functions since each data point can only use a selection of weak learners, instead of all of them. This model generalization is accomplished by including a binary weight matrix in the conditional distribution of the response variable, which activates only a specific subset of decision trees for each observation. Such a matrix is endowed with an Indian Buffet process prior, and sampled within the MCMC sampler, together with the other BART parameters. We then compare the Infinite BART model with the classic one on simulated and real datasets. Specifically, we provide examples illustrating variable importance, partial dependence and causal estimation.
items.authors: Marco Battiston, Yu Luo

items.title: Nonparametric Stochastic Subspaces via the Bootstrap Method for Characterizing Model Error
items.abstract: Reliable forward uncertainty quantification in engineering requires methods that account for aleatory and epistemic uncertainties. In many applications, epistemic effects arising from uncertain parameters and model form dominate prediction error and strongly influence engineering decisions. Because distinguishing and representing each source separately is often infeasible, their combined effect is typically analyzed using a unified model-error framework. Model error directly affects model credibility and predictive reliability; yet its characterization remains challenging. To address this need, we introduce a bootstrap-based stochastic subspace model for characterizing model error in the stochastic reduced-order modeling framework. Given a snapshot matrix of state vectors, the method leverages the empirical data distribution to induce a sampling distribution over principal subspaces for reduced order modeling. The resulting stochastic model enables improved characterization of model error in computational mechanics compared with existing approaches. The method offers several advantages: (1) it is assumption-free and leverages the empirical data distribution; (2) it enforces linear constraints (such as boundary conditions) by construction; (3) it requires only one hyperparameter, significantly simplifying the training process; and (4) its algorithm is straightforward to implement. We evaluate the method's performance against existing approaches using numerical examples in computational mechanics and structural dynamics.
items.authors: Akash Yadav, Ruda Zhang

items.title: Consistent and scalable detection and comparison of spatial patterns
items.abstract: Spatial omics maps molecular features within tissues to study their organization across biological contexts, including disease and development. Interpreting these maps requires distinguishing patterns from noise and comparing them across samples. Yet pattern detection remains unresolved, and comparisons based on regional summaries lose spatial detail. Here we show that spatial frequency provides a common basis for detecting and comparing these patterns. Our framework, SONIC, unifies spatial detection tests through a common quadratic form, establishes conditions for reliable detection and explains how kernel choice determines sensitivity to different spatial patterns. It also separates changes in spatial organization from changes in overall abundance without aligning tissues. Fast, memory-efficient algorithms make detection and comparison practical across large datasets. Applying SONIC, we identify plaque-associated responses in Alzheimer's disease and differences in the spatial expression of blood-clotting genes between glioma subtypes. We further construct a gene-centric atlas that traces changes in spatial expression through mouse and human embryogenesis and supports retrieval of related patterns across species. These results extend spatial analysis from identifying individual patterns to following their changes across anatomically different tissues. Together, SONIC establishes a shared language for integrating molecular maps across studies and technologies.
items.authors: Jiayu Su, Jun Hou Fung, Haoyu Wang, Dian Yang, Xiao Wang, David A. Knowles, Raul Rabadan

items.title: Consensus-level substitution rates are distinct from the virion-level rate
items.abstract: Estimating viral substitution rates is central to evolutionary epidemiology, and recent interest in within-host evolution has sharpened the question of what such rates measure. I distinguish two classes of evolutionary rate estimand that are rarely separated in phylogenetic analysis: the virion-level substitution rate (VLSR), a molecular quantity counting mutational events along lineages, and consensus-level substitution rates (CLSRs), population-summary quantities counting allele frequency threshold crossings from below. CLSRs are indexed by the consensus-generation rule. The VLSR and CLSRs are both biologically meaningful, but not interchangeable. Because the consensus-generation rule defines a given CLSR, it should be reported routinely. This reflection should help analysts make more informed methodological choices when working with sets of virus sequences.
items.authors: David J Pascall

items.title: Continuous-Speech Parkinson's Disease Detection Using Acoustic and Inharmonicity Features
items.abstract: Notable efforts have been made to identify Parkinson's disease (PD) from vocal data, primarily using sustained vowel phonations. In this work, we extend on these efforts introducing a PD identification approach for continuous speech, enabling a practical background monitoring of voice data to detect vocal changes indicative of PD. Using two distinct data sets, we compare the best sustained vowel model with that of the proposed continuous speech model, clearly illustrating the preferential performance of the latter. We examine approaches for speaker level evaluation and data leakage preventions, as well as how vowel information may be reliably extracted from continuous speech. The proposed method framework exploits both traditional acoustic representations and a promising novel inharmonicity based framework, showing how the latter provides complementary information improving the performance for one of the data sets; however, for the other data set, this information did not significantly improve (nor reduce) the performance, suggesting that further studies are required before being able to draw firm conclusions in its use.
